docs.title: Flow Bedrock
docs.text:
Initial version: 2026-10-12 · First published: 2026-10-13 · Last content update: 2026-10-18

This note documents a small ODE-based simulator I built to develop intuition for flow models (continuous normalizing flows / flow matching) and their relationship to diffusion models (typically defined via SDEs), with this update adding conditional control and 3D probability transport.

In deterministic mode, the simulator evolves particles under a time-dependent velocity field by numerically integrating an ODE. Each particle has a position \(X_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(d=2\) for the 2D demos and \(d=3\) for the 3D demos. Learned sampling runs from noise at \(t=0\) to the target at \(t=1\):

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}X_t}{\mathrm{d}t}=v(X_t,t), \qquad t\in[0,1], \qquad X_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_d). \tag{1} \]

The velocity field can be specified by hand or learned from data. In the conditional demo, the learned field also takes a control label \(c\) as input, so the velocity becomes \(v_\theta(X_t,t,c)\). The label is held fixed throughout each sampling run.

The analytic ring can continue beyond \(t=1\). The stochastic mode adds Brownian motion and a score correction to the learned flow, as described in Section 1.3.

It is primarily a visualization tool: trajectories and particle clouds make the abstract objects in the math (vector fields, marginal distributions, and couplings between source and target distributions) easier to reason about.

  • Particles as data samples. In the simulator, each particle is one sample \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\). In a larger generative model, a sample may represent an image, an audio segment, a motion sequence, or another object encoded as numerical data or a latent representation. Diffusion and flow models are not limited to images. The animation shows the evolution of a population of samples; a visible particle is not a pixel or a semantic part of a generated object.
  • Toy shapes as structured distributions. The 2D examples are an analytic ring, a learned PS5-like outline, and a learned Golden Ring pattern. Their point clouds concentrate around geometric structures with nonzero width. The Golden Ring pattern includes overlapping rings and image-derived texture, giving it more structure than a single smooth one-dimensional manifold. In 3D, the sampled targets likewise have nonzero thickness around spatial structures. In the learned examples, the model fits a probability distribution, including how mass is distributed around these shapes.
  • Analogy to real data. High-dimensional data can exhibit structure and correlations that concentrate probability mass near lower-dimensional subsets. This is a useful modeling perspective, not an assumption required by flow matching. Training learns a velocity field (or, in diffusion, a score or denoiser) from the data distribution. A finite-time ODE flow with a smooth flow map and smooth inverse preserves absolute continuity and cannot map a full-dimensional source density exactly onto a strictly lower-dimensional set; finite-thickness targets avoid implying such an exact collapse.
  • Conditional generation as control. Conditional models learn a distribution \(p_{\mathrm{data}}(x\mid c)\). In this demo, a ring label specifies a target conditional distribution and enters the learned velocity field during integration; it is not a filter applied to the completed particle cloud. Text-conditioned models use a representation of a prompt as the condition, while other applications may use class labels or other information. The shared mechanism is that the condition changes the generation dynamics. The demo's discrete ring labels illustrate this mechanism without implementing language understanding, and extending the state from 2D to 3D leaves the ODE formulation unchanged.

docs.title: What is on the screen?
docs.text:
Each visible point is one sample \(X_t\in\mathbb{R}^d\), with \(d=2\) or \(d=3\). The complete particle cloud is a finite empirical approximation to a probability distribution at time \(t\).

The recorded 2D demos use:

Control Value Meaning n_sim 100,000 particles advanced by the backend n_vis 10,000 particles sampled and sent to the browser dt 0.01 simulated time advanced per backend update steps 2 numerical substeps per update h 0.005 substep size, \(h=\texttt{dt}/\texttt{steps}\) hz 15 requested backend update rate

The backend evolves all 100,000 particles on an NVIDIA RTX 5090. Only 10,000 particles are streamed to the browser. The stream number in the HUD is the measured backend broadcast rate; it is not the browser's rendering FPS.

The optional density layer is computed from the displayed subsample. It is a binned, log-scaled visualization, not an exact normalized density. It is off by default in the clean presentation setup. A rendering overlay changes what is drawn, not the transport field or the particle law.

docs.title: 1.1 Hand-Crafted Velocity Field: Ring
docs.text:
The first stage uses an analytic vector field. No neural network or checkpoint is involved.

For \(x=(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb{R}^2\), define

\[ r=\lVert x\rVert_2, \qquad \rho=\max(r,10^{-4}), \qquad r_\star(t)=1.7+0.2\sin(2\pi t). \tag{2} \]

The non-rotating ring field is

\[ u_t(x) =0.8\bigl(r_\star(t)-\rho\bigr) \frac{x}{\rho}. \tag{3} \]

This field is radial negative feedback. For nonzero points inside the target radius, it pushes particles outward; outside that radius, it pulls them inward. The origin remains fixed. There is no tangential component. For a nonzero trajectory, write \(r_t=\|X_t\|_2\). Its polar angle obeys

\[ \frac{d\theta_t}{dt} =\frac{X_{t,1}u_{t,2}(X_t)-X_{t,2}u_{t,1}(X_t)}{r_t^2}=0. \]

Thus particles can move inward or outward without rotating. The numerical safeguard \(\rho\) changes the radial speed near zero but does not introduce angular motion.

The simulator solves the ordinary differential equation

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}X_t}{\mathrm{d}t}=u_t(X_t). \tag{4} \]

For a fixed time \(t\), the ideal circle

\[ \mathcal{M}_t=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^2:\lVert x\rVert_2=r_\star(t)\} \tag{5} \]

is a smooth one-dimensional manifold embedded in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). This makes the ring a useful geometric baseline: its ideal shape is simpler than a textured outline or a pattern of intersecting rings.

Along a particle trajectory, write \(r_t=\lVert X_t\rVert_2\). Whenever \(r_t\ge10^{-4}\), the ODE implies

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}r_t}{\mathrm{d}t}=0.8\bigl(r_\star(t)-r_t\bigr). \tag{6} \]

The field attracts particles toward the target radius, but does not bring the entire cloud exactly onto it in a finite run. Since the target radius changes with time, particles also show a tracking lag: at \(r_t=r_\star(t)\), their instantaneous radial velocity is zero even while the target circle may be expanding or shrinking. The animation shows a distribution with radial spread around the ideal circle. A smooth, invertible ODE flow cannot collapse a full-dimensional Gaussian distribution exactly onto a one-dimensional circle in finite time.

The simulation clock in this analytic example can continue past \(t=1\). The radius schedule is periodic, so the ring can keep changing radius even though its particles do not rotate. This is not a learned sampler with a fixed terminal state at 1.

The earlier recording used \(u_t^{\mathrm{old}}(x)=u_t(x)+1.5(-x_2,x_1)\), so its angular velocity was 1.5 radians per unit simulation time. Removing this term preserves the radial equation (6). For an isotropic Gaussian initial law, rotational symmetry also means that the ideal continuous-time marginal distributions are unchanged, despite different individual trajectories. This conclusion does not hold for an arbitrary anisotropic initial cloud, and finite numerical samples need not coincide.

Recording pending review

The existing archived ring recording shows the earlier rotating field. It is not embedded as a demonstration of equation (3). The live source, an isolated GPU integration, and the live Safari display were checked on 2026-10-18. The replacement browser recording is still pending; it must show no moving foreground light, no angular rotation, and the density layer disabled.

docs.title: 1.2 Learned Velocity Field: A PS5-Like Outline
docs.text:
The ring example writes geometric rules directly into a velocity field. For the PS5-like controller outline, we instead learn a field \(v_\theta:\mathbb{R}^2\times[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^2\) from target samples.

The target is a distribution of two-dimensional coordinates representing a controller outline. The PS5 checkpoint uses a preprocessed point set derived from the outline; the sampler centers and scales these coordinates, then draws target points with Gaussian jitter. The image below shows the reference shape:

This reference outline illustrates the target geometry. Preprocessing produces a point set, and sampling defines the probability distribution around it. The picture alone does not specify how probability mass is assigned to the coordinates.

The velocity network receives only a point and a time, and predicts a two-dimensional velocity. The PS5 checkpoint uses an MLP with four hidden layers of width 256 and SiLU activations, taking three scalars \((x_1,x_2,t)\) as input and returning two velocity components. The mask and its preprocessing settings are not network inputs.

The visible point cloud forms a recognizable outline, but each point remains one sample in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). With positive Gaussian jitter, the target has a two-dimensional density concentrated near the sampled outline. With zero jitter and a finite set of base coordinates, the sampler instead defines a discrete target law. This example learns coordinate statistics, rather than generating pixels or identifying the controller's semantic parts.

docs.title: Training: Construct a Path and Regress Its Velocity
docs.text:
Sample the source endpoint, target endpoint, and time independently:

\[ X_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_2), \qquad X_1\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, \qquad T\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]. \tag{7} \]

For a sampled endpoint pair, define the training path

\[ Y_t=(1-t)X_0+tX_1, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}Y_t}{\mathrm{d}t}=X_1-X_0, \qquad t\in[0,1]. \tag{8} \]

The endpoints make the supervision easy to compute: the velocity along this particular straight path is simply their displacement. Training minimizes

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RF}}(\theta) =\mathbb{E}\!\left[ \left\lVert v_\theta(Y_T,T)-(X_1-X_0)\right\rVert_2^2 \right]. \tag{9} \]

The expectation is over all three independent draws. Assuming finite second moments, the population-optimal predictor is

\[ v^\star(x,t) =\mathbb{E}[X_1-X_0\mid Y_t=x], \tag{10} \]

for each fixed \(t\), up to sets of zero probability under the law of \(Y_t\). Squared-error regression returns this conditional mean because its error decomposes into the predictor's squared distance from the conditional mean and a residual variance independent of the predictor.

The endpoint pair is used to construct a training example; it is not supplied to the network. Many pairs can produce intermediate states near the same location and time, so the learned field averages their displacement information. Consequently, the straight training paths do not force generated trajectories to be straight.

The following snippet shows one training step. base_points is a tensor of shape [M, 2] with \(M\ge1\), already centered and scaled; jitter_std is the positive standard deviation used by the target sampler. The model, tensors, and optimizer state use the same device:

# Draw independent source and target samples.
x0 = torch.randn(batch_size, 2, device=device)
idx = torch.randint(base_points.shape[0], (batch_size,), device=device)
x1 = base_points[idx]
x1 = x1 + jitter_std * torch.randn_like(x1)

# Build one intermediate state and its target velocity per pair.
t = torch.rand(batch_size, 1, device=device)
yt = (1.0 - t) * x0 + t * x1
target_velocity = x1 - x0

predicted_velocity = model(yt, t)
loss = (predicted_velocity - target_velocity).square().sum(dim=1).mean()
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

The loss above matches the squared Euclidean norm in the formula. The implementation uses nn.MSELoss(), which averages over both samples and the two output coordinates, giving half this value. This constant factor leaves the population minimizer unchanged.

docs.title: Generation: Integrate the Frozen Field
docs.text:
After training, freeze the network and draw fresh Gaussian samples. Generation solves

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}\widehat{X}_t}{\mathrm{d}t} =v_\theta(\widehat{X}_t,t), \qquad \widehat{X}_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_2), \qquad t\in[0,1]. \tag{11} \]

Here \(Y_t\) denotes the constructed training interpolant, while \(\widehat{X}_t\) denotes a trajectory obtained by integrating the learned field. No target endpoint is assigned to a generated particle, and no parameter update takes place during sampling. Unlike the continuously running analytic ring, this learned demo uses the checkpoint's time interval and stops at \(t=1\).

Loading the checkpoint reconstructs the network and restores its weights. Sampling then runs with the model in evaluation mode and gradients disabled. At each RK4 substep, the solver queries the frozen network at several intermediate positions and times; it does not interpolate each particle toward a stored target point. Time advances through \([0,1]\) and stops at the endpoint.

The PS5 recording uses deterministic ODE sampling with RK4 and zero diffusion amplitude. With the initial seed and numerical settings fixed, replay compares the same initial samples under the same learned field. The final cloud approximates the training distribution; finite model capacity, optimization error, numerical integration, and finite sample size all limit agreement. A recognizable silhouette alone does not establish that the probability mass within the silhouette is correct.

This video records the live particle canvas at 30 fps using the browser's captureStream and MediaRecorder APIs. It includes a parameter label drawn for the recording; the control panel and hardware HUD are separate page elements and are not captured. The particle positions come from the running backend simulation. The clip shows the Gaussian start, the learned transport, and a pause at the final outline.

docs.title: 1.3 Stochastic Paths with the Same Time Marginals
docs.text: The previous PS5 example transports Gaussian samples with a deterministic ODE. We now add random motion while aiming to retain the same evolving distributions. The cloud still develops into the controller outline, but individual samples follow noisy paths. This lets us compare deterministic and stochastic probability transport using the same target geometry.

docs.title: Add Noise and Compensate for Its Effect
docs.text:
Let \(p_t(x)\) be the density of the training interpolant \(Y_t=(1-t)X_0+tX_1\), with \(x\in\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). The velocity network approximates a field transporting this path; a second network estimates the score of the same path,

\[ s_\phi(x,t)\approx s_t(x)= abla_x\log p_t(x). ag{12} \]

For a deterministic scalar diffusion schedule \(g(t)\) that depends only on time, the demo integrates the Itô SDE

\[ \mathrm{d}Z_t =\left[v_ heta(Z_t,t)+ rac{1}{2}g(t)^2s_\phi(Z_t,t) ight]\mathrm{d}t +g(t)\,\mathrm{d}W_t, \qquad Z_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_2), ag{13} \]

Here \(Z_t\in\mathbb{R}^2\) denotes the stochastic sample, and \(W_t\) is standard Brownian motion in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), independent of \(Z_0\). Adding noise alone would change the density evolution. The positive score correction is chosen to compensate for that diffusion at the level of one-time distributions.

To see the cancellation, replace the learned fields by exact \(v_t\) and \(s_t= abla_x\log p_t\), where \(v_t\) satisfies the continuity equation for \(p_t\). With sufficiently smooth positive densities, suitable decay at infinity, and well-posed dynamics, the Fokker–Planck equation gives

\[ egin{aligned} \partial_t p_t &=- abla\!\cdot\!\left[ \left(v_t+ rac{1}{2}g^2 abla\log p_t ight)p_t ight] + rac{1}{2}g^2\Delta p_t\ &=- abla\!\cdot(v_t p_t). \end{aligned} ag{14} \]

The extra terms cancel because \(( abla\log p_t)p_t= abla p_t\) and \(g\) is independent of position. Starting from the same source law, the exact ODE and this SDE therefore share the same density at every time. Their individual trajectories and path-space laws remain different. The endpoint distribution is the final member of this family of time marginals.

docs.title: Learn the Score of the Entire Path
docs.text:
The required score belongs to the evolving path, rather than only its endpoint. Because \(X_0\) is standard Gaussian and independent of \(X_1\),

\[ \begin{aligned} Y_t\mid X_1&\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(tX_1,(1-t)^2I_2\right),\\ \left.\nabla_y\log p_t(y\mid X_1)\right|_{y=Y_t} &=-\frac{X_0}{1-t},\qquad 0\le t<1. \end{aligned} \tag{15} \]

Averaging the conditional score given \(Y_t=y\) yields the marginal score \(s_t(y)\). The path-score network uses the weighted regression objective

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{score}}(\phi) =\mathbb{E}\!\left[ \left\lVert(1-T)s_\phi(Y_T,T)+X_0\right\rVert_2^2 \right], \qquad T\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,0.99], \tag{16} \]

with \(T\) independent of both endpoints. The interval excludes the singular conditional-score limit at \(t=1\).

docs.title: The Recorded Stochastic Demo
docs.text:
The comparison video uses the same PS5 velocity checkpoint, seed 42, initial samples, and visible sample indices in both runs. Each run advances 100,000 samples and displays 10,000 of them. Three samples are highlighted in matching colours, with polylines joining their actual streamed positions. Their paths make the difference visible even when the overall clouds look similar.

The left panel uses the deterministic ODE with Euler integration. The right panel adds the path-score correction and random increments, using Euler–Maruyama and the diffusion amplitude

\[ g(t)= \begin{cases} 0.6\left(1-\dfrac{t}{0.99}\right),&0\le t<0.99,\\ 0,&0.99\le t\le1. \end{cases} \tag{17} \]

The larger noise amplitude makes the path differences easier to inspect and decreases to zero as sampling progresses. Both panels use the same internal step size \(h=0.005\). Euler also handles the right panel's final deterministic interval. This comparison keeps the drift discretization consistent; the earlier standalone ODE video in Section 1.2 uses RK4. During the stochastic interval, let \(Z_k\) be the numerical state at time \(t_k\). For a step of length \(h>0\), Euler–Maruyama uses

\[ Z_{k+1}=Z_k+ \left[v_\theta(Z_k,t_k)+\frac{1}{2}g(t_k)^2s_\phi(Z_k,t_k)\right]h +g(t_k)\sqrt{h}\,\varepsilon_k, \qquad \varepsilon_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_2), \tag{18} \]

where the Gaussian increments are independent across steps and particles. The \(\sqrt{h}\) factor is essential: Brownian increments have covariance \(hI_2\).

Watch the coloured paths: the ODE paths vary smoothly, while the SDE paths show irregular turns and backtracking. Both clouds still approach the controller outline. The video combines two live canvas recordings; the labels report each run's numerical settings and simulation time. The coloured trails are a visualization of sampled trajectories, rather than additional forces or noise added during editing.

Both the learned fields and the numerical integration are approximate. Increasing \(g_{\mathrm{peak}}\) also amplifies the contribution of score error through the factor \(g^2/2\). The checkpoint metadata contains inconsistent jitter values, so this recording is a qualitative demonstration rather than a verification of exact marginal equality or an exactly matched training distribution.

docs.title: 2. Golden Ring: Conditional Control
docs.text:
The PS5 example learns one target distribution. Golden Ring adds a new question: can one velocity network generate different parts of a structured target when we change a control label?

The complete target contains three overlapping rings, a vertical structure, and fine image-derived texture. We first sample coordinates from the full image, then define three additional target distributions using ring-shaped selection masks. One network learns all four branches: the full target, the central ring, the left-tilted ring, and the right-tilted ring.

docs.title: 2.1 From a Coloured Image to a Target Distribution
docs.text:
The image supplies sampling weights rather than network inputs. For pixel \(i\) in the finite image index set \(\mathcal{I}\), let \(b_i\in[0,1]^3\) be its RGB vector and define the intensity heuristic

\[ \ell_i=0.2126b_{i,1}+0.7152b_{i,2}+0.0722b_{i,3}. \tag{19} \]

The implementation weights pixels by intensity and similarity to a chosen gold colour:

\[ w_i=\mathbf 1_{\{\ell_i\ge\tau\}}\,\ell_i^{\gamma_\ell} \exp\!\left(-\frac{\lVert b_i-b_\star\rVert_2^2}{2\sigma_{\mathrm{col}}^2}\right), \tag{20} \]

where \(b_\star=(214,164,95)/255\), corresponding to #d6a45f. The checkpoint uses \(\tau=0.02\), \(\gamma_\ell=1\), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{col}}=0.35\). Bright pixels near this colour receive larger sampling weights. These operations use the stored RGB values as a sampling heuristic, rather than estimating physical radiance.

Let \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^2\) be the resulting pixel coordinates after an isotropic spatial scaling, a shared centering step, and the final target normalization. The isotropic scaling preserves the image's aspect ratio. A target sample is a selected coordinate plus isotropic Gaussian jitter with standard deviation \(\delta=0.01\). The network learns the resulting coordinate distribution; it sees neither the source image nor its RGB values.

This first clip uses the full-target branch and shows Gaussian samples developing into the complete pattern. The target has thickness, intersections, and texture. Its geometry is more complex than a single smooth one-dimensional manifold.

docs.title: 2.2 Four Target Laws in One Coordinate System
docs.text:
Write the control token as \(C\in\{0,1,2,3\}\):

Token Demo label Target used for training \(0\) Full distribution all pixels with positive full-image sampling weight \(1\) R1: central ring full-image weights restricted by the central-ring mask \(2\) R2: left-tilted ring full-image weights restricted by the left-ring mask \(3\) R3: right-tilted ring full-image weights restricted by the right-ring mask

Let \(m_{i,c}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether pixel \(i\) belongs to the selection mask for token \(c\), with \(m_{i,0}=1\). The normalized pixel probabilities are

\[ \pi_i^{(c)}=\frac{w_i m_{i,c}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}w_jm_{j,c}}, \qquad c\in\{0,1,2,3\}, \tag{21} \]

assuming each denominator is positive. With \(J\mid C=c\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\pi^{(c)})\) and independent \(\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_2)\), the sampled target is

\[ \begin{aligned} X_1&=a_J+\delta\varepsilon,\\ p_{\mathrm{data}}(x\mid c) &=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\pi_i^{(c)}\, \mathcal{N}(x;a_i,\delta^2I_2),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^2. \end{aligned} \tag{22} \]

Here \(\mathcal{N}(x;a_i,\delta^2I_2)\) denotes a Gaussian density evaluated at \(x\). Positive jitter gives each branch a two-dimensional density concentrated near its selected structure, with Gaussian tails extending beyond the mask.

The masks can overlap. They select weighted coordinates before jitter is added, and all branches share the full image's coordinate center and scale. This keeps each ring in its original spatial location. The full target also contains structure outside these masks, so its distribution is separately sampled; it is not assumed to equal a mixture of the three ring distributions.

docs.title: 2.3 Learn a Conditional Velocity Field
docs.text:
Training retains the straight interpolant from Section 1.2. Draw \(X_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_2)\) independently of \((C,X_1)\), draw \(X_1\) from the selected target law, and draw \(T\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) independently of all other variables. Define

\[ Y_t=(1-t)X_0+tX_1, \qquad t\in[0,1], \tag{23} \]

and minimize

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cond}}(\theta) =\mathbb{E}\!\left[ \left\lVert v_\theta(Y_T,T,C)-(X_1-X_0)\right\rVert_2^2 \right]. \tag{24} \]

With finite second moments, the population-optimal predictor for each token is

\[ v^\star(x,t,c)=\mathbb{E}[X_1-X_0\mid Y_t=x,C=c], \tag{25} \]

up to sets of zero probability under the corresponding path law. The endpoint pair supplies the regression target. The control label selects the target law and remains an input during generation.

The V5 trainer allocates half of each batch to token \(0\), sampling the full target directly. For the remaining half, it chooses uniformly among the three ring labels. Thus the full-target branch is explicitly trained alongside the conditional branches. The implementation calls token \(0\) the unconditional token; here that means the full-image target, rather than a marginal formed by combining the three ring labels.

The network uses six hidden layers of width 768 with SiLU activations, four Fourier frequencies per spatial coordinate, and a learned 16-dimensional token embedding. Its input combines position, time, spatial Fourier features, and the token embedding; its output remains a two-dimensional velocity.

The following code shows the regression step for one chosen token. base_points has shape [M, 2] and contains the shared centered and scaled coordinates; weights has shape [M], and masks has shape [3, M]. Each masked weight sum is positive. All tensors and the model use the same device, and c is an integer in 0..3. The full trainer mixes these groups within each batch:

# Define the target law for this token, then sample coordinates.
q = weights if c == 0 else weights * masks[c - 1]
q = q / q.sum()
idx = torch.multinomial(q, batch_size, replacement=True)
x1 = base_points[idx] + 0.01 * torch.randn(batch_size, 2, device=device)

# Source samples and time are independent of the target draw.
x0 = torch.randn_like(x1)
t = torch.rand(batch_size, 1, device=device)
yt = (1.0 - t) * x0 + t * x1
control = torch.full((batch_size,), c, dtype=torch.long, device=device)

predicted_velocity = model(yt, t, control)
loss = torch.nn.functional.mse_loss(predicted_velocity, x1 - x0)
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

As in Section 1.2, mse_loss gives half the squared-norm batch average because it also averages over the two output coordinates.

docs.title: 2.4 The Label Changes the Entire Flow
docs.text:
To generate samples for a fixed token \(c\), freeze the network and solve

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}\widehat{X}_t^{(c)}}{\mathrm{d}t} =v_\theta(\widehat{X}_t^{(c)},t,c), \qquad \widehat{X}_0^{(c)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_2), \qquad t\in[0,1]. \tag{26} \]

The mask has already served its purpose in preparing training samples. At inference, the ring label enters every velocity evaluation, including RK4's intermediate stages. Every sample is transported under the selected field; particles are not deleted or filtered after generating the full pattern.

The comparison clip reuses the same seed, initial Gaussian cloud, visible sample indices, camera, and integration settings. It runs R1, R2, and R3 from \(t=0\) in turn. The changing trajectories and endpoint shapes therefore reflect the label-dependent field, rather than a different initialization or a separately loaded model.

Both clips use deterministic ODE sampling, RK4 with internal step size \(h=0.005\), 100,000 simulated samples, 10,000 displayed samples, and seed 42. Each run reaches \(t=1\) before its final frame is held for inspection. The recordings capture the live canvas with an added label showing which branch is active. Agreement with the target distribution remains approximate because the field is learned and sampling is numerical.

docs.title: 2.5 What the CFG Scale Means
docs.text:
The full-target branch also supplies the baseline for classifier-free guidance. To keep it distinct from the score notation in Section 1.3, write the guidance scale as \(\lambda\ge0\). For \(c\in\{1,2,3\}\), the implemented field is

\[ v_{\mathrm{CFG}}(x,t,c;\lambda) =v_\theta(x,t,0) +\lambda\left[v_\theta(x,t,c)-v_\theta(x,t,0)\right]. \tag{27} \]

At \(\lambda=0\) this is the full-target field; at \(\lambda=1\) it is the learned conditional field. Values above one extrapolate in the direction of the conditional-minus-full velocity. They can strengthen the visual condition, but do not guarantee a more accurate target distribution. The recorded comparisons fix \(\lambda=1\) throughout.

These labels are discrete geometric conditions. They demonstrate how a shared network changes its transport field when given a condition. A richer conditioning system could supply a learned representation of text or other information, while retaining the same conditional ODE structure.

docs.title: 3. Probability Transport in 3D
docs.text: The 3D demos keep the same flow-matching construction and change the ambient space from \(\mathbb{R}^2\) to \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Each sample now has three coordinates, and the network predicts three velocity components. A rendered frame is a perspective projection of those samples; rotating the camera reveals the depth that a single projection can hide.

docs.title: 3.1 The Same Objective in Three Coordinates
docs.text:
For each target, independently sample \(X_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_3)\) and \(X_1\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}\), with \(T\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) independent of both. Define \(Y_t=(1-t)X_0+tX_1\) for \(t\in[0,1]\). The training objective is

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{3D}}(\theta) =\mathbb{E}\left[ \left\lVert v_\theta(Y_T,T)-(X_1-X_0)\right\rVert_2^2 \right], \qquad v_\theta:\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,1]\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^3. \tag{28} \]

As in Section 1.2, squared-error regression has the population optimum \(v^*(x,t)=\mathbb{E}[X_1-X_0\mid Y_t=x]\), defined almost everywhere under the interpolant distribution. The training segment \(Y_t\) supplies a velocity target; generated trajectories follow the learned field instead:

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}\widehat{X}_t}{\mathrm{d}t} =v_\theta(\widehat{X}_t,t), \qquad \widehat{X}_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_3), \qquad t\in[0,1]. \tag{29} \]

These demos use three separately trained networks, one for each target. Unlike Golden Ring's conditional branches, switching the 3D target loads a different checkpoint. Each network is an MLP with five hidden layers of width 512 and SiLU activations. Its input is \((x_1,x_2,x_3,t)\) and its output is a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Trefoil was trained for 15,000 steps; Swiss Roll and Double Helix for 10,000 each, all with batch size 32,768, learning rate \(2\times10^{-4}\), and training seed 42.

The training step has the same structure as the 2D example:

# One 3D target sampler and one velocity network per experiment.
source = torch.randn(batch_size, 3, device=device)
target = sample_target(batch_size, device=device)  # shape: (B, 3)
time = torch.rand(batch_size, 1, device=device)
interpolant = (1.0 - time) * source + time * target
prediction = model(interpolant, time)
loss = (prediction - (target - source)).square().sum(dim=1).mean()
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()

This snippet implements the squared vector norm exactly. The trainer uses elementwise mean squared error, which is \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{3D}}/3\) in three dimensions and has the same population minimizer.

docs.title: 3.2 Trefoil: A Tube Around a Knotted Curve
docs.text:
The Trefoil centerline is the closed curve

\[ \gamma_{\mathrm{tr}}(\phi) =\sqrt{\frac35} \begin{pmatrix} (2+\cos 3\phi)\cos 2\phi\\ (2+\cos 3\phi)\sin 2\phi\\ \sin 3\phi \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \phi\in[0,2\pi). \tag{30} \]

The sampler distributes centerline positions approximately uniformly in arc length. In the continuum, this corresponds to a parameter density proportional to \(\lVert\gamma'_{\mathrm{tr}}(\phi)\rVert_2\). The implementation inverts a cumulative chord-length table with 16,384 intervals.

At each sampled position, let \(n_1(\phi),n_2(\phi)\) be an orthonormal basis perpendicular to the unit tangent. With \(Q\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) and \(A\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,2\pi)\) independent of each other and of \(\Phi\), the target sample is

\[ X_1=\gamma_{\mathrm{tr}}(\Phi) +0.14\sqrt{Q}\left[\cos A\,n_1(\Phi)+\sin A\,n_2(\Phi)\right]. \tag{31} \]

The square root makes each cross-section uniform in disk area: the radial cumulative distribution is \(\Pr(R\le r)=(r/0.14)^2\) for \(0\le r\le0.14\). The target is a solid tube around a one-dimensional centerline. Arc-length sampling and uniform disks define its probability law; curvature means this construction is not exactly uniform in ambient tube volume.

The rotating endpoint view exposes the over-and-under arrangement of the knot. An apparent crossing in one image is a crossing of projected points, rather than an intersection of the centerline in three dimensions.

docs.title: 3.3 Swiss Roll: A Thickened Surface
docs.text:
The Swiss Roll mid-surface is

\[ F(u,y)= \begin{pmatrix} a u\cos u\\ y\\ a u\sin u \end{pmatrix}, \qquad u\in\left[\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{9\pi}{2}\right], \quad y\in[-1.35,1.35], \quad a=0.14. \tag{32} \]

Its area element is \(a\sqrt{1+u^2}\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}y\). Accordingly, the sampler draws \(U\) with density proportional to \(\sqrt{1+u^2}\) on the stated interval and draws \(H\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[-1.35,1.35]\) independently. The cumulative distribution of \(U\) is numerically inverted using the primitive

\[ \int\sqrt{1+u^2}\,\mathrm{d}u =\frac{1}{2}\left[u\sqrt{1+u^2}+\operatorname{arsinh}(u)\right]+\text{constant}. \tag{33} \]

Writing \(x(u)=au\cos u\) and \(z(u)=au\sin u\), choose the unit normal

\[ n(u)=\frac{(-z'(u),0,x'(u))^{\mathsf T}}{a\sqrt{1+u^2}}. \tag{34} \]

An independent signed offset \(B\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[-0.07,0.07]\) gives \(X_1=F(U,H)+B\,n(U)\). The mid-surface is two-dimensional and has boundary; the sampled target is a three-dimensional slab of total normal thickness \(0.14\). The mid-surface sampling is area-balanced, while the normal-offset construction specifies the slab density without claiming uniform ambient volume.

The camera rotation makes the separate turns and their gaps visible. Points on different turns can overlap in a projection while remaining separated in space.

docs.title: 3.4 Double Helix: Two Thick Strands
docs.text:
For an arm index \(j\in\{0,1\}\), define

\[ \gamma_{\mathrm{hel},j}(\phi)= \begin{pmatrix} 1.25\cos(\phi+j\pi)\\ 1.25\sin(\phi+j\pi)\\ \dfrac{3.6}{4\pi}\phi-1.8 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \phi\in[0,4\pi]. \tag{35} \]

The sampler chooses each arm with probability \(1/2\) and draws \(\Phi\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,4\pi]\) independently. Each arm makes two turns and has constant centerline speed, so uniform \(\Phi\) also gives uniform centerline arc length. The endpoints lie at heights \(-1.8\) and \(1.8\).

The same normal-disk construction adds a cross-section of radius \(0.13\), followed by independent isotropic Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(0.015\):

\[ X_1=\gamma_{\mathrm{hel},J}(\Phi) +0.13\sqrt{Q}\left[\cos A\,n_{J,1}(\Phi)+\sin A\,n_{J,2}(\Phi)\right] +0.015\,\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_3). \tag{36} \]

Here the normal vectors are orthonormal and perpendicular to the corresponding arm's tangent; \(Q,A,\varepsilon\) are independent of each other and of \((J,\Phi)\). The Gaussian term gives the target density nonzero tails outside the two compact tubes. This example models a geometric point distribution; it carries no molecular dynamics or interaction law.

docs.title: 3.5 What the Recordings Demonstrate
docs.text:
All three clips start from the same seeded Gaussian samples and visible indices, use deterministic RK4 sampling with \(h=0.005\), and evolve 100,000 samples while displaying 10,000. The camera is fixed during transport from \(t=0\) to \(t=1\). Once transport finishes, the sample coordinates remain fixed and the camera rotates for six seconds. The caption identifies this change, so viewing motion is distinguishable from probability transport.

The ideal centerlines and mid-surface have lower intrinsic dimension, while the training targets have finite thickness in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). This distinction matters for the ODE interpretation. A sufficiently regular velocity field with a globally defined invertible flow transports an absolutely continuous source to another absolutely continuous distribution; it cannot collapse that source exactly onto a curve or surface in finite time. Moreover, such a flow preserves full support, so the compact Trefoil and Swiss Roll targets can only be approximated by these regular learned flows at the endpoint. Their visible shapes show concentration near the intended geometry, with finite model and integration error.

The 3D extension therefore changes the sample space and target geometry while preserving the flow-matching objective. Camera rotation helps inspect spatial structure; quantitative distributional accuracy would require separate evaluation beyond these visual demonstrations.

docs.title: Guidance and classifier-free guidance — How conditioning changes sampling
docs.text:
Initial version: 2026-10-28 · First published: 2026-10-29 · Last content update: 2026-10-28

Literature checked through 2026-10-28; recent preprints are identified separately.

A conditional generator already receives the requested condition during training and sampling. Guidance introduces a further choice: whether to use its conditional prediction directly or modify the sampling field to emphasize the condition. These choices need to be separated, because stronger condition adherence, better perceptual quality, and more accurate sampling of the conditional data distribution are different objectives.

We follow the progression used in the MIT course notes, Chapter 5: vanilla conditioning, classifier guidance, and classifier-free guidance. Here, “vanilla” means ordinary conditional generation, not unconditional generation. Conditioning on a prompt or class is also distinct from conditioning on a sampled endpoint when constructing flow-matching training paths.

docs.title: 1. Vanilla conditioning: learn the conditional field directly
docs.text:
Let \((X_0,Y)\) have the data joint law, with \(X_0\in\mathbb R^d\) and condition \(Y\in\mathcal Y\). In this chapter, \(t\in[0,T]\) runs in the forward noising direction, from data toward noise; generation traverses these times backwards. This differs from the noise-to-data convention used in our flow-matching examples.

For a Gaussian corruption, write

\[ X_t=\alpha_tX_0+\sigma_t\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d), \qquad \varepsilon\perp(X_0,Y). \tag{1} \]

The condition stays fixed while the data state changes.

\((X_0,Y)\) is a pair of random variables with the data joint law: a data sample and its associated condition. The notation \(\varepsilon\perp(X_0,Y)\) means that the Gaussian noise is drawn independently of the entire pair; it does not mean that the data and condition are independent of each other. Equation (1) corrupts only the data state, not the condition.

For a fixed condition \(y\), a typical implementation computes \(e_y=\operatorname{Encoder}(y)\) once per generation and reuses it in every prediction \(\varepsilon_\theta(X_t,t,e_y)\). The embedding stays fixed while \(X_t\) and \(t\) change. Its effect need not stay fixed: in cross-attention, for example, queries depend on the current state, so attention weights can change even when the condition embedding does not.

A fixed embedding during one sampling run is a common implementation choice, not a mathematical requirement. It also does not imply that the condition encoder is frozen during training. We write \(\varepsilon_\theta(x,t,y)\) below as shorthand that includes the encoding of \(y\).

The coefficients are fixed schedules. Statements involving division by \(\sigma_t\) apply only where \(\sigma_t>0\). Let \(p_t(x\mid y)\) denote the resulting conditional density. A conditional noise predictor is trained with

\[ \mathcal L_{\mathrm{cond}}(\theta) = \mathbb E\!\left[ \|\varepsilon_\theta(X_t,t,Y)-\varepsilon\|^2 \right], \tag{2} \]

where the expectation also samples time from a chosen training distribution, independently of data and noise. Assuming finite second moments and sufficient model capacity, its population optimum is

\[ \varepsilon^*(x,t,y) =\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X_t=x,Y=y], \qquad s_t^{\mathrm c}(x,y) :=\nabla_x\log p_t(x\mid y) =-\frac{\varepsilon^*(x,t,y)}{\sigma_t}. \tag{3} \]

The score identity follows by differentiating the Gaussian mixture density, wherever differentiation under the integral is justified. Providing \(y\) changes the conditional expectation being learned; the training target remains the sampled noise. With the exact conditional score, the appropriate reverse dynamics, and the correct terminal law, conditional generation does not require an additional amplification step. A shared Gaussian initialization is an approximation unless the terminal noising law actually removes dependence on \(y\).

docs.title: 2. Classifier guidance: obtain the conditional correction through Bayes' rule
docs.text:
For clarity, take \(Y\) to be a discrete class and fix \(y\) with positive probability. Where the densities are positive and differentiable,

\[ p_t(x\mid y)= rac{p_t(x)p_t(y\mid x)}{p(y)}, ag{4} \]

so

\[ s_t^{\mathrm c}(x,y) = \underbrace{ abla_x\log p_t(x)}_{s_t^{\mathrm u}(x)} + \underbrace{ abla_x\log p_t(y\mid x)}_{ ext{conditional correction}}. ag{5} \]

The derivative of \(\log p(y)\) vanishes because it does not depend on \(x\). A time-dependent classifier \(c_\phi(y\mid x,t)\) can estimate the second term. It must handle the noisy states encountered at time \(t\); a classifier trained only on clean data does not automatically estimate this posterior.

The unconditional-base form of classifier guidance is

\[ s_{\mathrm{CG}}(x,t,y) =s_ heta^{\mathrm u}(x,t) +\gamma abla_x\log c_\phi(y\mid x,t). ag{6} \]

With exact models, \(\gamma=1\) recovers the conditional score. Choosing \(\gamma>1\) amplifies its conditional correction; this is a sampling modification rather than the Bayes identity itself. Classifier guidance can also be added to an already conditional base model, in which case the baseline and scale convention must be adjusted. Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) develop classifier-guided diffusion sampling and examine its quality–diversity trade-off.

docs.title: 3. Classifier-free guidance: estimate the correction without a separate classifier
docs.text:
Rearranging the same identity gives

\[ \nabla_x\log p_t(y\mid x) =s_t^{\mathrm c}(x,y)-s_t^{\mathrm u}(x). \tag{7} \]

Thus two generative predictions can supply the correction. During training, independently replace the condition with a reserved null token \(\varnothing\) with probability \(\rho\in(0,1)\). Training on both retained and dropped conditions lets a single network estimate conditional and unconditional predictions. Independent dropping is important: the dropped subset should retain the marginal data law.

At sampling time, combine the predictions:

\[ s_{\mathrm{CFG}}(x,t,y) =s_\theta(x,t,\varnothing) +\gamma\left[s_\theta(x,t,y)-s_\theta(x,t,\varnothing)\right]. \tag{8} \]

Under our convention, \(\gamma=0\) gives the unconditional prediction, \(\gamma=1\) the ordinary conditional prediction, and \(\gamma>1\) extrapolates beyond it. The original CFG paper also uses the form \((1+w)s_{\mathrm c}-ws_{\mathrm u}\), corresponding to \(\gamma=1+w\). Noise predictions admit the same linear combination when their noise scale and parameterization agree. “Classifier-free” removes the separate classifier, not the conditioning information or the usual two branch evaluations. Ho and Salimans (2022).

docs.title: 4. A local score identity does not identify the generated endpoint distribution
docs.text:
For exact scores and a constant \(\gamma\), define, when the normalizer is finite,

\[ r_t(x\mid y) =\frac{p_t(x\mid y)^\gamma p_t(x)^{1-\gamma}}{Z_t(y)}, \qquad Z_t(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_t(x\mid y)^\gamma p_t(x)^{1-\gamma}\,dx. \tag{9} \]

At each fixed time,

\[ \nabla_x\log r_t(x\mid y) =\gamma s_t^{\mathrm c}(x,y)+(1-\gamma)s_t^{\mathrm u}(x). \tag{10} \]

This is a spatial derivative identity. It does not establish that the family \(r_t\) satisfies the forward Fokker–Planck equation associated with the original noising process. Consequently, replacing its reverse sampler's score with this expression does not generally produce \(r_0\). The missing requirement is consistency across time, not a missing normalization constant in the spatial gradient.

Bradley and Nakkiran, Classifier-Free Guidance is a Predictor-Corrector (2024 preprint; TMLR 2025) analyze this distinction and show that CFG interacts differently with DDPM and DDIM. Their SDE-limit analysis connects CFG to denoising plus a Langevin sharpening correction. This directly qualifies the tempting claim that CFG simply samples a powered conditional distribution.

The same caution applies when comparing guided ODE and SDE samplers: their unguided probability-flow correspondence cannot simply be assumed to survive an arbitrary score modification. For flow matching, linear combinations of conditional and unconditional velocities can be implemented, but the score derivation above is not by itself a theorem identifying their output law.

docs.title: 5. Recent directions and reading map
docs.text:
The following papers address different design choices. Their reported improvements concern the models, samplers and evaluation settings studied; they are not universal guarantees.

Design choice Reference Contribution and role in this chapter When to apply guidance Applying Guidance in a Limited Interval Improves Sample and Distribution Quality in Diffusion Models, Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 Finds that restricting guidance to an intermediate noise interval improves results in the evaluated settings. Motivates a schedule rather than one constant scale throughout sampling. Which prediction to use as the reference Guiding a Diffusion Model with a Bad Version of Itself, Karras et al., 2024 Autoguidance uses a weaker version of the model rather than an unconditional model; also studies unconditional generation. Shows that guidance effects extend beyond enforcing a condition. How guidance enters a numerical update CFG++: Manifold-constrained Classifier Free Guidance for Diffusion Models, Chung et al., 2024 Revises the guidance update, motivated by off-manifold behavior, and reports improvements in generation and inversion. Its geometric explanation should be presented with its assumptions, not as a general law of data geometry. What distribution the sampler produces Classifier-Free Guidance is a Predictor-Corrector, Bradley and Nakkiran, 2024 / TMLR 2025 Establishes why the fixed-time powered-density score argument does not determine the endpoint law; central theoretical reading for Section 4. Whether two branches are needed at inference Diffusion Models without Classifier-free Guidance, Tang et al., 2025 Proposes Model-guidance, changing the training objective to avoid standard two-branch CFG inference. This moves work into training rather than providing a free replacement for every pretrained model. How to choose guidance weights Learn to Guide Your Diffusion Model, Galashov et al., 2025 / ICLR 2026 Learns weights depending on the condition and denoising interval by minimizing distributional mismatch; also considers reward-tilted targets. Makes the choice of evaluation objective explicit.

docs.title: October 2026 preprints to follow
docs.text:
These are recent proposals, not established explanations adopted by this chapter. The summaries below reflect their stated methods; their detailed theoretical assumptions and experiments still require a closer reading.

  • Opening the Black Box of Classifier-Free Guidance via Information Bottleneck, Gao et al., October 2026. Proposes an information-theoretic account of when conditioning is useful and an adaptive guidance activation rule. Relevant to the interval-guidance discussion.
  • TrajCFG: Token-Wise Classifier-Free Guidance via Denoising Trajectory Feedback, Liu et al., October 2026. For flow-matching models, adapts token-wise guidance scales using historical changes in velocity direction, reusing ordinary CFG predictions without additional model evaluations. Relevant to replacing one global guidance scale with local allocation.

For the first reading pass, prioritize the two original guidance papers, the predictor-corrector analysis, interval guidance, and learned guidance weights. Autoguidance and the newer preprints then broaden the discussion without interrupting the vanilla → classifier → classifier-free derivation.

docs.title: \(\alpha\)1. A classical fluid-mechanics brief
docs.text:
Timeline and the world

1) Calculus (late 1600s)

2) Montesquieu and The Spirit of Laws (1748)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spirit_of_Laws

3) Diderot, d’Alembert, and the Encyclopédie (1751)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A9die

4) Voltaire and the Lisbon earthquake (1755) - Event: the 1755 Lisbon earthquake. - Links: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire | https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1755_Lisbon_earthquake

5) Euler in Berlin (1755–1757) - Why this is “genesis” for fluid dynamics: fluids are treated as continuous fields, not discrete particles. - Academic note: Euler formalizes \( ho\) (density) and \(p\) (pressure) as spatial fields and writes down the inviscid equations we still use today. - Primary source: Euler, L. (1757). “Principes généraux du mouvement des fluides”. Mémoires de l'Académie des Sciences de Berlin. - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_equations_(fluid_dynamics)

Close of this brief: the modern “flow matching” story is basically a machine-learning re-telling of classical transport, learn a time-dependent vector field, then integrate its trajectories. - Eulerian viewpoint: describe the whole medium by fields over space-time. - State variables live on space-time: \( ho(x,t)\) (density), \(v(x,t)\) (velocity), and often \(p(x,t)\) (pressure) and/or \(e(x,t)\) (internal energy). - Think “field snapshot”: at any fixed \(t\), you can draw arrows \(v(\cdot,t)\) and a scalar map \( ho(\cdot,t)\). Motion is encoded by how those fields evolve in \(t\). - The bridge to particle motion is the trajectory / characteristic \(x(t)\) that satisfies \(\dot x(t)=v(x(t),t)\). Along that path, the rate of change of any field \(f(x,t)\) is the material derivative (Eq. (1)).

  • That single operator \(D/Dt\) is the conceptual hinge: Eulerian fields + Newtonian time evolution.

  • Newton’s laws as constraints (continuum mechanics viewpoint):

  • Setup: take any control volume \(\Omega\) fixed in space with boundary \(\partial\Omega\) and outward normal \(n\). Newton’s laws apply to the mass and momentum in that volume.

  • Mass conservation (a separate balance law, with no mass sources): integral form (Eq. (2)), differential form (Eq. (3)).

  • Momentum conservation (Newton’s 2nd law, \(F=ma\)):

    Integral form (Eq. (4)).

    Here \(b(x,t)\) is body force per unit mass (e.g., gravity), and \(\sigma(x,t)\) is the Cauchy stress tensor encoding surface forces.

  • Angular-momentum balance implies a symmetric Cauchy stress tensor in the classical continuum without body couples or couple stresses: \(\sigma=\sigma^ op\). Action–reaction alone is not the full justification for this symmetry.

  • For an inviscid fluid (no shear stress), stress reduces to isotropic pressure: \(\sigma = -p I\). Plugging this into the momentum balance yields the Euler equations:

    Differential form (Eq. (5)).

    The acceleration term \(\partial_t v + (v\cdot abla)v\) is exactly \(Dv/Dt\): Newton’s law written in Eulerian coordinates. - Closure: mass + momentum are not enough; you typically need an equation of state \(p=p( ho,\ldots)\) and/or an energy equation. (For many ML “flow” analogies we keep only the kinematic core: a vector field that transports density.)

Numbered equations:

Work in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), with time in an interval \([0,T]\). The control volume \(\Omega\) is fixed in space and has a piecewise smooth boundary with outward unit normal \(n\). Assume sufficiently regular fields, no mass sources, and no body couples or couple stresses. Here \( ho\) is mass density, \(v\) velocity, \(b\) body force per unit mass, \(\sigma\) Cauchy stress, and \(p\) physical pressure.

Material derivative

\[ rac{D f}{D t} = \partial_t f + v\cdot abla f. ag{1} \]

Mass conservation (integral form)

\[ rac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega} ho\,dx = -\int_{\partial\Omega} ho v\cdot n\,dS. ag{2} \]

Continuity equation (differential form)

\[ \partial_t ho + abla\cdot( ho v)=0. ag{3} \]

Momentum balance (integral form)

\[ egin{aligned} rac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega} ho v\,dx &+\int_{\partial\Omega} ho v\,(v\cdot n)\,dS\ &=\int_{\Omega} ho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega}\sigma n\,dS. \end{aligned} ag{4} \]

Correction (2026-10-14). The previous fixed-control-volume equation omitted the momentum carried through its boundary. The flux term in (4) is required because fluid crosses the fixed boundary. A volume moving with the fluid instead has a material-volume formulation. The accompanying stress-symmetry statement now invokes angular-momentum balance under the stated classical assumptions. See the Sandia balance-law derivation, Sections 8.3–8.4.

Euler equations (inviscid, differential form)

\[ ho ig(\partial_t v + (v\cdot abla)v ig) = - abla p + ho b. ag{5} \]

How flow models reuse this math (vs. what remains “physics constraints”):

  • What a flow model actually uses (kinematics / transport):
  • A learned time-dependent vector field \(v_ heta(x,t)\) defines an ODE \(\dot x(t)=v_ heta(x(t),t)\) (characteristics).
  • Probability mass is transported by that field through the continuity / Liouville equation (Eq. (3)). This is the backbone behind CNFs and flow matching: it tells you how \( ho(x,t)\) changes when particles move with velocity \(v\).
  • A commonly used derived identity along trajectories is the log-density evolution:
    • \( rac{d}{dt}\log ho(x(t),t) = - abla\cdot v(x(t),t)\).
    • This is just Eq. (3) rewritten on characteristics (and is where the \( abla\cdot v\) term in continuous normalizing flows comes from).

  • Eq. (1) (material derivative) is often used as notation to make these “along a trajectory” statements compact, but it is not an extra assumption.

  • What is mostly not enforced in ML flows (dynamics / constitutive physics):

  • Eq. (4) and Eq. (5) become relevant only if you want \(v\) to be physically correct for an actual fluid (pressure, stress, body forces, plus a closure / equation of state).
  • In generative modeling, \(v_ heta\) is typically free to be whatever field best transports \(p_0 o p_1\); we do not solve for \(p\) or \(\sigma\) and we do not impose Newtonian momentum balance unless we are doing physics-informed modeling.

docs.title: Section B — Flow Matching as the default protagonist
docs.text:
Initial version: 2026-02-05 · Last content update: 2026-10-17

Flow models use the mathematics of deterministic probability transport: a velocity field defines trajectories, and those trajectories transform a source law into a model law. The trajectories have no assumed physical meaning. Training selects the field; sampling integrates its ODE.

Notation used throughout. Data states lie in \(\mathbb R^d\). Generation runs from source at \(t=0\) toward data at \(t=1\); formulas with a singular endpoint are stated for \(t<1\).

Symbol Meaning \(X_t\), \(x\) A random vector and a deterministic state; uppercase denotes random vectors. \(\mu_0,\mu_{\mathrm{data}}\); \(p=p_0,q\) Source and target probability laws; their densities, when they exist. \(\mu_t\); \(p_t\) A probability path and its density: \(\mu_t(dx)=p_t(x)\,dx\). \(u_t(x)\); \(u_{\theta,t}(x)\) A specified transport field (the regression target in B2); its learned approximation. \(\psi_t\); \(\psi_{\theta,t}\) ODE flow maps generated by \(u_t\) and \(u_{\theta,t}\), respectively. \(\mu_{\theta,t}\); \(p_{\theta,t}\) The learned sampler's law and density; equality to \(\mu_t,p_t\) is a fitting goal. \(\pi_{0,1}\); \(\gamma_t(x_0,x_1)\) An endpoint coupling and a chosen interpolation map; neither prescribes the marginal ODE's individual trajectories. \(p_{t\mid 1}(x\mid x_1)\); \(p_{1\mid t}(x_1\mid x)\) The density of \(X_t\) given \(X_1=x_1\), and the reverse conditional density. \(\rho,v,P,\boldsymbol{\sigma},\tau,y\) Physical mass density, velocity, pressure, stress tensor, time, and position; used only in the fluid comparison.

We write \(X\sim p\) as shorthand for a law with density \(p\), but use measures in pushforwards and set probabilities. All densities are relative to Lebesgue measure unless a different reference measure is specified; density identities hold almost everywhere, or pointwise under the stated smoothness assumptions. Unmarked spatial derivatives act on the displayed state variable: \(\nabla_x\) is a scalar gradient, \(D_xu\) is the vector-field Jacobian with \((D_xu)_{ij}=\partial u_i/\partial x_j\), and \(\Delta_x\) is the Laplacian. Dots denote differentiation in the displayed time parameter. A conditioning bar indicates a conditional law or expectation; in \(\gamma_t(x_0\mid x_1)\), it only marks \(x_1\) as a fixed parameter of the interpolation map.

docs.title: B0. Section goal
docs.text:
• Treat flow/ODE as the mainline
  • Training = learn a vector field
  • Sampling = numerical integration (Euler/Heun/RK)

Source notation: \(u_t^\theta\) corresponds to \(u_{\theta,t}\) here. In the embedded caption, “source distribution \(q\)” is a typo: the source is \(p\), as shown in the panels.

docs.title: Interlude \(\alpha\) — Year 1757
docs.text:
• interlude-alpha-year-1757.md

Introducing a flow turns learning a data distribution into choosing a transformation of a simple random input. The connection to fluid mechanics is useful only if we distinguish the equations that describe transport from the equations that determine the transporting field. A trajectory equation says how to follow a given field. Newton's momentum balance restricts that field through forces. FM selects a field through a training objective. These are different roles, and the assumptions below support different steps in this construction.

docs.title: Trajectories from a given velocity field
docs.text:
Used by FM: the sampling equation. Let \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), \(t\in[0,1]\), and \(u_t(x)\in\mathbb R^d\), with initial point \(a\in\mathbb R^d\). In FM, \(x\) represents a complete data state, and \(t\) is a chosen generation parameter; neither needs the physical meaning or units of position and time. Giving a velocity field means specifying the instantaneous rate of change at every state and time. A trajectory must accumulate those changes while evaluating the field at its current position:

\[ \dot x_t=u_t(x_t),\qquad x_0=a, \qquad x_t=a+\int_0^t u_s(x_s)\,ds. \tag{I.1} \]

The integral form follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus. It explains the connection between a local rate and a whole path; it does not establish existence or uniqueness. The initial state is needed because the same field can carry different starting points along different paths. We impose uniqueness so that the ODE specifies an entire sampling trajectory from each initial state without an additional solution-selection rule. The regularity conditions used below are sufficient for this purpose; they are not necessary conditions for every possible sampler. No force law or inertial mass enters this requirement.

docs.title: Mass conservation and Newton's second law
docs.text:
In a fluid, the velocity field is itself an unknown. We need to predict which field develops, not merely follow a field already supplied. In an inertial frame, let \(y\in\mathbb R^3\) denote physical position, \( au\in[0,T]\) with \(T>0\) physical time, \( ho>0\) mass density, \(v\) velocity, \( oldsymbol{\sigma}\) Cauchy stress, and \(b\) body force per unit mass. Assume smooth fields and no mass sources. For any material volume \(V( au)\), whose boundary moves with the fluid, the two balance laws are

\[ egin{aligned} rac{d}{d au}\int_{V( au)} ho\,dy&=0,\ rac{d}{d au}\int_{V( au)} ho v\,dy &=\int_{V( au)} ho b\,dy +\int_{\partial V( au)} oldsymbol{\sigma} n\,dS. \end{aligned} ag{I.2} \]

The first equation is mass conservation; the second is Newton's momentum balance: momentum change rate equals total force. Here \(n\) is the outward unit normal on the relevant boundary. The quantity \( oldsymbol{\sigma} n\) is force per unit area exerted across that boundary. The body-force integral and the surface-traction integral are therefore the two contributions to the total force. These are physical balance laws being assumed, not consequences of defining a velocity field.

The transport theorem converts a derivative over a moving volume into local accumulation and transport terms. The divergence theorem converts surface force into a volume integral. Since the balances hold for every material volume, their local forms are

\[ egin{aligned} \partial_ au ho+ abla_y\cdot( ho v)&=0,\ \partial_ au( ho v)+ abla_y\cdot( ho v\otimes v) &= abla_y\cdot oldsymbol{\sigma}+ ho b. \end{aligned} ag{I.3} \]

Reused structure: continuity, with probability replacing physical mass. FM uses the first equation's transport structure, replacing \(( ho,v, au,y)\) by a probability density and sample-space field \((p_t,u_t,t,x)\). Its justification will be preservation of probability under a map. FM does not impose the second equation, momentum balance, on its field.

Here \((v\otimes v)_{ij}=v_i v_j\), and tensor divergence differentiates the second index. Expanding the left side of momentum balance shows exactly where mass conservation is used:

\[ egin{aligned} \partial_ au( ho v)+ abla_y\cdot( ho v\otimes v) &= ho igl[\partial_ au v+(v\cdot abla_y)v igr]\ &\quad+v\underbrace{ igl[\partial_ au ho+ abla_y\cdot( ho v) igr]}_{0}. \end{aligned} ag{I.4} \] \[ egin{aligned} ho rac{Dv}{D au} &= abla_y\cdot oldsymbol{\sigma}+ ho b,\ rac{Dv}{D au}&:=\partial_ au v+(v\cdot abla_y)v. \end{aligned} ag{I.5} \]

The material derivative \(Dv/D au\) of velocity is acceleration along a moving fluid element. The term \((v\cdot abla_y)v\) appears because that element encounters different local velocities as it changes position, even when the field is steady. The material-derivative identity is the chain rule and also applies to a smooth FM field; equating mass density times acceleration to force is the additional physical law. Newton's law relates this acceleration to force per unit volume.

docs.title: The additional assumptions of incompressible Euler flow
docs.text:
Physical constraints not imposed by ordinary FM. Choose constant density \( ho_0>0\), no body force, and isotropic pressure stress:

\[ egin{gathered} ho= ho_0,\qquad b=0,\qquad oldsymbol{\sigma}=-PI,\ oldsymbol{\sigma} n=-Pn,\qquad abla_y\cdot oldsymbol{\sigma}=- abla_yP. \end{gathered} ag{I.6} \]

Here \(P\) is pressure and \(I\) the identity matrix. For positive \(P\), the minus sign represents compressive traction acting inward. Unequal pressure on opposite faces leaves a net force; the spatial difference becomes the pressure gradient. The relation \( oldsymbol{\sigma}=-PI\) omits viscous stress. Neither this stress model nor constant density follows from Newton's law. Substituting these choices into the balance laws gives the incompressible Euler equations:

\[ oxed{ abla_y\cdot v=0,\qquad \partial_ au v+(v\cdot abla_y)v=- rac{1}{ ho_0} abla_yP.} ag{I.7} \]

Constant density makes mass conservation require equal local inflow and outflow, hence zero divergence. To specify a concrete evolution problem, take a bounded, connected container \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3\) with a smooth, stationary, impermeable wall. Prescribe a smooth initial velocity \(v_0\) that is divergence-free and tangent to the wall:

\[ v(y,0)=v_0(y),\qquad v\cdot n ig|_{\partial\Omega}=0. ag{I.8} \]

The initial field specifies the motion already present; an evolution equation alone cannot select it. The wall condition prevents crossing the boundary and permits tangential slip in this inviscid model. Pressure must produce an acceleration that preserves both zero divergence and zero wall-normal velocity. For a smooth solution, taking the divergence and the wall-normal component of momentum balance yields

\[ egin{aligned} \Delta_yP&=- ho_0 abla_y\cdot igl[(v\cdot abla_y)v igr] && ext{in }\Omega,\ \partial_nP&=- ho_0 n\cdot igl[(v\cdot abla_y)v igr] && ext{on }\partial\Omega, \end{aligned} ag{I.9} \]

where \(\partial_nP=n\cdot abla_yP\). The Neumann compatibility condition holds because the divergence theorem makes the volume integral of the prescribed Laplacian equal to the boundary integral of the prescribed normal derivative. Given an admissible current velocity, pressure is therefore determined up to a spatial constant at each time; that constant may depend on \( au\). Its gradient determines the velocity's time derivative through momentum balance, on the interval where a smooth solution exists. This is the extra field-solving problem imposed by this physical model. Integrating trajectories in a known field does not solve it. Ordinary FM imposes neither these Euler equations nor this pressure boundary-value problem. It does not obtain its field by setting physical mass or forces to zero; those physical variables are absent from its formulation.

Changed problem: learn a transport between distributions. FM specifies a base probability law \(\mu_0\) and a target law \(\mu_{\mathrm{data}}\), then learns a field over the generation interval. It does not evolve a prescribed initial velocity \(v_0\) under Newton's law. Each generated sample still needs an initial state \(X_0\sim\mu_0\). In the sample space \(\mathbb R^d\) used here, there is no container wall and hence no wall boundary condition.

docs.title: Mathematical conditions for a complete sampling trajectory
docs.text:
Sufficient mathematical assumptions for ODE sampling. Return to the sample-space field \(u_t(x)\). Assume continuity in time and local Lipschitz continuity in space, uniformly on compact time-space sets. These conditions justify the deterministic sampler analyzed here; they are not physical laws or necessary conditions for every FM formulation. Choose a closed ball of radius \(r>0\) around \(a\), with spatial Lipschitz constant \(L\) and a velocity bound \(B_u\), uniform over a compact time interval near zero. For continuous curves in that ball, the integral update \((\mathcal T x)_t=a+\int_0^t u_s(x_s)\,ds\) satisfies

\[ \lVert\mathcal T x-\mathcal T z\rVert_\infty \le Lh\,\lVert x-z\rVert_\infty, \qquad 0\le t\le h. \tag{I.10} \]

Here the norm is the supremum over \([0,h]\). Choose \(h\) within that time interval with \(B_u h\le r\) and \(Lh<1\). The first bound keeps the update in the ball; the second makes it a contraction on the complete space of continuous curves taking values there. Repeated updates therefore converge to a unique fixed point: the local trajectory. More generally, Grönwall's inequality bounds separation between two trajectories remaining in a common compact region:

\[ \lVert x_t-z_t\rVert\le e^{Lt}\lVert x_0-z_0\rVert. \tag{I.11} \]

Equal initial states have zero initial separation, so their futures cannot separate. This is the reason for the uniqueness assumption. Continuity alone is insufficient: for the continuous scalar field \(u(x)=2\sqrt{\max\{x,0\}}\), both staying at zero and waiting until any \(c\in[0,1]\) before following \(x_t=(\max\{t-c,0\})^2\) solve the ODE with \(x_0=0\).

Local uniqueness does not ensure that sampling reaches \(t=1\). The smooth field \(u(x)=x^2\), starting at \(x_0=2\), gives \(x_t=2/(1-2t)\) for \(0\le t<1/2\), and diverges at \(t=1/2\). A sufficient way to exclude such escape is a uniform linear-growth bound with a finite constant \(C\ge0\):

\[ \begin{gathered} \lVert u_t(x)\rVert\le C(1+\lVert x\rVert),\qquad C\ge0,\\ \Longrightarrow\quad \lVert x_t\rVert+1\le(\lVert x_0\rVert+1)e^{Ct}. \end{gathered} \tag{I.12} \]

Combined with local existence, this finite bound permits continuation throughout \([0,1]\). To establish invertibility, we need both uniqueness and existence of a backward trajectory from every terminal point. For a fixed \(t\in[0,1]\) and any \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), solve

\[ \frac{d\eta_s}{ds}=-u_{t-s}(\eta_s),\qquad \eta_0=x, \qquad 0\le s\le t. \tag{I.13} \]

This reversed field satisfies the same local Lipschitz and growth bounds, so \(\eta_t\) exists uniquely. It gives \(\psi_t^{-1}(x)=\eta_t\), where \(\psi_t(a)=x_t\). Thus every terminal point has exactly one initial point. Invertibility is a consequence of these forward and backward ODE guarantees. This is stronger than merely saying that trajectories do not merge, which establishes injectivity but not surjectivity.

docs.title: Probability transport and density formulas
docs.text:
Used by FM: the law of generated samples. If \(X_0\) has probability law \(\mu_0\), define \(X_t=\psi_t(X_0)\). For every measurable set \(A\),

\[ \mu_t(A):=\mathbb P(X_t\in A) =\mu_0 igl(\psi_t^{-1}(A) igr), \qquad \mu_t=(\psi_t)_\#\mu_0. ag{I.14} \]

Normalization is inherited: \(\mu_t(\mathbb R^d)=\mu_0(\mathbb R^d)=1\). This fact needs only a measurable map defined on the initial samples; invertibility is not necessary for a general sampler.

Extra assumptions for a density formula. Invertibility and differentiability become useful when we want a pointwise density formula. If \(D_xu\) is jointly continuous, differentiating the trajectory with respect to its initial point gives, for \(J_t(a)=D_a\psi_t(a)\),

\[ egin{gathered} \dot J_t=D_xu_t(\psi_t(a))J_t,\qquad J_0=I,\ \det J_t=\exp\!\left(\int_0^t abla_x\cdot u_s(\psi_s(a))\,ds ight)>0. \end{gathered} ag{I.15} \]

The Jacobian determinant measures how a small transported volume expands or contracts. If the initial law has a density \(p_0\), preserving the probability in that volume gives the change-of-variables formula, almost everywhere:

\[ p_t(\psi_t(a))\det J_t(a)=p_0(a). ag{I.16} \]

These Jacobian formulas describe how the density changes. The FM regression loss below does not require evaluating a density or a Jacobian determinant.

Used by FM: the probability continuity equation. The same transport can be expressed without following individual initial points. For a smooth, compactly supported test function \(\varphi\), the chain rule and integration by parts give

\[ egin{aligned} rac{d}{dt}\int\varphi(x)p_t(x)\,dx &=\mathbb E[ abla\varphi(X_t)\cdot u_t(X_t)]\ &=\int abla\varphi(x)\cdot u_t(x)p_t(x)\,dx, \end{aligned} ag{I.17} \] \[ \Longrightarrow\quad oxed{\partial_tp_t+ abla_x\cdot(p_tu_t)=0.} ag{I.18} \]

All integrals are over \(\mathbb R^d\); compact support removes the boundary term. The PDE holds weakly, and classically when the density is sufficiently smooth. This derivation uses neither Newton's law nor a stress model. It is probability bookkeeping for a deterministic transformation. Probability conservation does not require \( abla_x\cdot u_t=0\). FM may use nonzero divergence to change density along trajectories; the incompressible fluid example forbids that volume change.

docs.title: Learning a field that reaches the target distribution
docs.text:
The preceding results would also hold for a smooth field that produces the wrong data distribution. Exact generation additionally requires \((\psi_1)_\#\mu_0=\mu_{\mathrm{data}}\). This condition does not generally identify a unique motion. For example, in two dimensions the standard Gaussian density \(g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1}e^{-\lVert x Vert^2/2}\) is preserved both by zero velocity and by rotation \(w(x)=\omega(-x_2,x_1)\), with constant \(\omega\in\mathbb R\), since

\[ abla_x\cdot(gw)= abla_xg\cdot w+g abla_x\cdot w =-g\,x\cdot w+0=0. ag{I.19} \]

Thus even an entire density path can leave motion undetermined. FM uses this freedom to construct training examples with known velocities.

Training choices: a coupling and an interpolation. One simple construction takes independent endpoint draws \(Z_0\sim\mu_0\) and \(Z_1\sim\mu_{\mathrm{data}}\) with finite second moments. The chosen linear interpolation has a directly computable derivative:

\[ S_t=(1-t)Z_0+tZ_1,\qquad V:=\dot S_t=Z_1-Z_0, \qquad u_t:=\operatorname{Law}(S_t). ag{I.20} \]

The endpoint laws are correct by construction: \( u_0=\mu_0\) and \( u_1=\mu_{\mathrm{data}}\). Endpoint independence and straight interpolation are choices in this example, not requirements of FM. Finite second moments ensure that the velocity label \(V\) is square-integrable here. This does not mean that each paired line must become a learned ODE trajectory. Different pairs can pass through the same state with different velocities. A field taking only \((x,t)\) as input must reconcile those labels.

Used by FM: conditional-mean regression. For each fixed \(t\), define the conditional mean \(m_t\) up to \( u_t\)-null sets. Using a jointly measurable version, a square-integrable predictor, and a time \(s\sim\mathcal U[0,1]\) independent of the endpoint pair, the regression identity is

\[ egin{aligned} m_t(x)&:=\mathbb E[V\mid S_t=x],\ \mathbb E\lVert u_{ heta,s}(S_s)-V Vert^2 &=\mathbb E\lVert u_{ heta,s}(S_s)-m_s(S_s) Vert^2\ &\quad+\mathbb E\lVert V-m_s(S_s) Vert^2. \end{aligned} ag{I.21} \]

These expectations include \(s,Z_0,Z_1\). The cross term vanishes because \(\mathbb E[V-m_s(S_s)\mid s,S_s]=0\). The second term is therefore independent of the predictor. Uniform time sampling is another training choice; the decomposition also holds with another independent time law, with equality to the minimizer required only almost everywhere under the resulting training measure. Among all square-integrable functions of state and time, the minimizer for the uniform choice is \(m_s\), up to \(ds\, u_s(dx)\)-null sets. A restricted neural-network family need not contain this minimizer; within that family the identity only reduces training to approximating \(m_s\).

Used by FM: the link from regression to probability transport. The reason the conditional mean is a valid transport candidate is that it preserves aggregate probability flux. For the same test functions as above,

\[ egin{aligned} rac{d}{dt}\mathbb E[\varphi(S_t)] &=\mathbb E[ abla\varphi(S_t)\cdot V]\ &=\mathbb E[ abla\varphi(S_t)\cdot m_t(S_t)]. \end{aligned} ag{I.22} \]

This establishes a weak continuity equation for \( u_t\) with field \(m_t\); it does not establish that \(m_t\) is locally Lipschitz or generates a unique ODE flow. The ODE assumptions are used again at this step: if a representative of \(m_t\) satisfies the stated time-continuity, local Lipschitz, and growth conditions on the whole closed interval, uniqueness of probability transport makes its exact ODE marginals equal to \( u_t\), including the target endpoint. A learned field \(u_{ heta,t}\) satisfying those same bounds also generates \( u_t\) if \(u_{ heta,t}=m_t\) almost everywhere under \(dt\, u_t(dx)\). This equality is sufficient, not necessary: different fields can transport the same marginal laws, as the rotation example shows. The regression identity does not guarantee regularity or exact learning. It identifies one target field; neither the identity nor interpolation alone proves that it has the required regularity or can be represented and learned exactly.

The conditions remain consequential: a \(C^1\) diffeomorphic flow starting from a law with a Lebesgue density still has a density at its endpoint. In \(\mathbb R^2\), it therefore cannot put probability one on a zero-width circle, which has zero area. Exact singular targets fall outside this regular, invertible endpoint setting; a construction aimed at such a target needs different assumptions, for example a justified singular endpoint limit. Finite model capacity, imperfect optimization, and numerical integration can also prevent exact matching. The logical separation is therefore essential: regularity defines a usable transport, the constructed path supplies regression targets, and the continuity equation explains when the learned field produces the desired distribution.

docs.title: Comparison of assumptions and equations
docs.text: The fluid model is the smooth, inviscid, constant-density Euler flow above: \(y\in\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3\), \(\tau\in[0,T]\), with a fixed impermeable boundary. FM uses \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), \(t\in[0,1]\). Assume sufficient smoothness and integrability for the displayed differential identities; the FM flow conditions are stated below.

docs.title: Conservation: a fixed mass versus total probability one
docs.text:
Let \(M>0\) be the total fluid mass. Let \(p_t\) be the density of the generated sample law \(\mu_t\), with initial density \(p_0\).

Quantity or equation Closed fluid system Deterministic probability transport Density \( ho(y, au)\ge0\) \(p_t(x)\ge0\) Initial total \(\int_\Omega ho(y,0)\,dy=M\) \(\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_0(x)\,dx=1\) Local continuity equation \(\partial_ au ho+ abla_y\cdot( ho v)=0\) \(\partial_tp_t+ abla_x\cdot(p_tu_t)=0\) Conserved total \(\int_\Omega ho(y, au)\,dy=M\) \(\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_t(x)\,dx=1\)

The constants differ: \(M\) has units of mass and, in the constant-density example, \(M= ho_0|\Omega|\). Total probability is dimensionless and equals one because the initial law is normalized. Neither statement says that a pointwise density equals one.

The boundary conditions needed to obtain these global integral identities from the PDE are explicit. For the fluid,

\[ rac{d}{d au}\int_\Omega ho\,dy =-\int_{\partial\Omega} ho v\cdot n\,dS=0, \qquad v\cdot n=0 ext{ on }\partial\Omega. ag{I.23} \]

For probability on \(\mathbb R^d\), put \(B_R=\{x:\|x\|<R\}\). If differentiation commutes with the \(R o\infty\) limit and the boundary flux vanishes,

\[ rac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathbb R^d}p_t\,dx =-\lim_{R o\infty}\int_{\partial B_R}p_tu_t\cdot n\,dS=0. ag{I.24} \]

The sampler also gives normalization directly, without this boundary-limit calculation: if \(\psi_t\) is measurable and defined \(\mu_0\)-almost everywhere,

\[ \mu_t=(\psi_t)_\#\mu_0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mu_t(\mathbb R^d)=\mu_0(\psi_t^{-1}(\mathbb R^d))=1. ag{I.25} \]

The exact correspondence is normalization of mass. On the physical domain, define \(r_ au(y)= ho(y, au)/M\). Since \(M\) is constant,

\[ egin{aligned} \int_\Omega r_ au(y)\,dy&=1,\ \partial_ au r_ au+ abla_y\cdot(r_ au v) &= rac{1}{M} igl[\partial_ au ho+ abla_y\cdot( ho v) igr]=0. \end{aligned} ag{I.26} \]

Thus \(r_ au\) is a probability density for a location selected in proportion to fluid mass. This gives the same transport equation for a normalized measure; it does not identify physical mass with probability or impose the fluid's momentum equation on FM.

Conservation is local flux balance, not just a fixed total. For fixed smooth subregions \(A\subset\Omega\) and \(B\subset\mathbb R^d\),

\[ egin{aligned} rac{d}{d au}\int_A ho\,dy &=-\int_{\partial A} ho v\cdot n_A\,dS,\ rac{d}{dt}\int_Bp_t\,dx &=-\int_{\partial B}p_tu_t\cdot n_B\,dS. \end{aligned} ag{I.27} \]

For a general compressible fluid or probability flow, these derivatives need not vanish. The constant-density Euler example imposes an additional restriction:

\[ ho= ho_0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \int_A ho\,dy= ho_0|A|,\qquad \int_{\partial A} ho_0v\cdot n_A\,dS=0 \quad ext{for every fixed }A. ag{I.28} \]

Fluid can cross that internal boundary, but total inflow equals total outflow. FM does not require this balance for each fixed region; its probability there can change.
