docs.title: Section C — Comparison table + code playbook
docs.text:
This section is a compact algorithm ↔ code playbook for three mainstream dynamics-based generative model families:

  • Score-based diffusion (SDE): learn a time-dependent score \(s_\theta(x,t)\) and sample with a reverse-time SDE (often with a predictor–corrector scheme), or deterministically via the probability-flow ODE.
  • Discrete diffusion (DDPM): learn a denoiser parameterization (commonly \(\varepsilon_\theta\)) and sample a reverse Markov chain.
  • Flow matching (ODE): learn a velocity field \(v_\theta(x,t)\) by regression and sample by ODE integration.

To avoid duplication, we keep derivations elsewhere:

  • Numerical ODE/SDE solvers: mathematics-foundation.md
  • Continuity / Fokker–Planck and reverse-time constructions: mathematics-foundation.md and diffusion-models-intro.md
  • Flow matching theory (CFM, Theorems 1–3, Gaussian paths): diffusion-models-intro.md and introduction-B-flow-matching.md

docs.title: C0. Notation (shared)
docs.text:
We work in \(\mathbb{R}^D\).

  • Data distribution: \(x_\text{data}\sim q(x)\) (we only have sample access).
  • Simple prior: \(x_\text{prior}\sim p(x)\) (often \(p=\mathcal{N}(0,I)\)).
  • Discrete time (DDPM): \(t\in\{1,\dots,T\}\).
  • Continuous time (SDE/ODE): \(t\in[0,1]\).
  • Model outputs:
  • score: \(s_\theta(x,t)\approx \nabla_x\log p_t(x)\),
  • noise: \(\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\approx\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid X_t=x_t]\) for each fixed \(t\), trained against the sampled noise in the forward noising formula,
  • velocity: \(v_\theta(x,t)\approx\mathbb{E}[\dot\gamma_t(X_0,X_1)\mid X_t=x]\), where \(X_t=\gamma_t(X_0,X_1)\). The sampled path derivative supplies the training label; the population-optimal field is its conditional mean.

docs.title: C1. Comparison table (what is modeled / learned / sampled)
docs.text: Aspect Score-based diffusion (SDE) Discrete diffusion (DDPM) Flow matching (ODE) Dynamics type Itô SDE \(dX_t=f(X_t,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t\) (forward), sample via reverse-time SDE (or PF-ODE) Forward Markov chain \(q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\) with designed \(\beta_t\), sample via reverse chain Deterministic ODE \(\frac{d}{dt}X_t=v_\theta(X_t,t)\) What is designed SDE coefficients \((f,g)\) / schedule (e.g., VP/VE) discrete schedule \(\beta_t\) (equiv. \(\alpha_t,\bar\alpha_t\)) a probability path (bridge) \(\gamma_t\) and a time grid What is learned \(s_\theta(x,t)\) (score), or equivalent parameterization typically \(\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\) (noise), sometimes \(x_{0,\theta}\) or \(v_\theta\) \(v_\theta(x,t)\) (velocity) Training inputs sample \((x_0,t)\), sample noise \(\varepsilon\), construct \(x_t\sim p_t(\cdot\mid x_0)\) in closed form sample \((x_0,t)\), sample noise \(\varepsilon\), construct \(x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon\) sample endpoints (noise/data) and time \(t\), construct \(x_t=\gamma_t(x_0,x_1)\) Supervision target closed-form conditional score \(\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t\mid x_0)\) (DSM) regression target \(\varepsilon\) in the forward corruption target velocity \(\dot\gamma_t(x_0,x_1)\) Sampling randomness stochastic (reverse SDE), or deterministic (PF-ODE) stochastic reverse chain (Gaussian transitions) deterministic ODE (any ODE solver) Typical solver Euler–Maruyama + Langevin corrector (PC), or ODE solver for PF-ODE ancestral time stepping Euler / Heun / RK methods (see mathematics-foundation.md)

docs.title: C2.1 Score-based diffusion (denoising score matching)
docs.text:
Assume a forward SDE is chosen so that the conditional \(p(x_t\mid x_0)\) is tractable (often Gaussian). Then the DSM objective regresses the model score to the closed-form conditional score:

\[ \mathbb{E}_{t,x_0,x_t}\Big[\lambda(t)\,\big\|s_\theta(x_t,t)-\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t\mid x_0)\big\|^2\Big]. \]

Pseudocode:

repeat:
  sample x0 ~ p_data
  sample t  ~ Uniform(0, 1)
  sample ε  ~ N(0, I)
  construct xt ~ p(xt | x0)   # e.g. VE: x0 + σ(t) ε ; VP: √α̅(t) x0 + √(1-α̅(t)) ε
  set target score s*(xt,t) = ∇_{xt} log p(xt | x0)  # closed form
  loss = λ(t) · || sθ(xt,t) - s*(xt,t) ||^2
  take optimizer step on loss w.r.t. θ

docs.title: C2.2 DDPM (noise-prediction loss)
docs.text:
DDPM training commonly regresses \(\varepsilon_\theta\) to the injected noise in the forward corruption:

repeat:
  sample x0 ~ p_data
  sample t  ~ Uniform({1, …, T})
  sample ε  ~ N(0, I)
  set xt = √α̅_t · x0 + √(1-α̅_t) · ε
  loss = || ε - εθ(xt, t) ||^2
  take optimizer step on loss w.r.t. θ

docs.title: C2.3 Flow matching (velocity regression on a designed path)
docs.text:
Choose a bridge \(\gamma_t(x_0,x_1)\) connecting a prior endpoint and a data endpoint, and regress a velocity field to the path derivative \(\dot\gamma_t\):

\[ \mathbb{E}_{t,(x_0,x_1)}\Big[\|v_\theta(\gamma_t(x_0,x_1),t)-\dot\gamma_t(x_0,x_1)\|^2\Big]. \]

For the linear bridge with \(x_0\sim p\), \(x_1\sim q\),

\[ \gamma_t(x_0,x_1)=(1-t)x_0+t x_1,\qquad \dot\gamma_t(x_0,x_1)=x_1-x_0. \]

Pseudocode:

repeat:
  sample x1 ~ p_data
  sample x0 ~ N(0, I)
  sample t ~ Uniform(0, 1)
  xt = (1 - t) · x0 + t · x1
  target = x1 - x0
  loss = || vθ(xt, t) - target ||^2
  take optimizer step on loss w.r.t. θ

Markov vs continuous path sampling (practical point). In DDPM, training pairs \((x_t,t)\) are generated from a discrete Markov chain and indexed by integer \(t\). In score-based diffusion and flow matching, \((x_t,t)\) is sampled from a continuous-time path in one shot (via a tractable conditional perturbation or an explicit interpolation), without a Markov constraint between adjacent times.

docs.title: C3.1 Score-based diffusion: predictor–corrector reverse-SDE sampler
docs.text:
initialize x ~ terminal prior  # VE: approximately N(0, σ_max² I); VP: approximately N(0, I)
for t = 1 → ε (descending):
  # Predictor: one reverse-SDE step (Euler–Maruyama)
  sample z ~ N(0, I)
  x ← x + [f(x,t) - g(t)^2 sθ(x,t)] Δt + g(t) √(|Δt|) · z

  # Corrector: K steps of Langevin at the same t (optional)
  repeat K times:
    sample z ~ N(0, I)
    x ← x + η_step · sθ(x,t) + √(2 η_step) · z
return x

The reverse-time formulas and the probability-flow ODE are summarized in diffusion-models-intro.md (Chapter 5.5) and in mathematics-foundation.md (Chapter 2).

docs.title: C3.2 DDPM: ancestral reverse diffusion
docs.text:
initialize x_T ~ N(0, I)
for t = T, …, 1:
  sample z ~ N(0, I) if t > 1 else 0
  mean = 1/√α_t · (x_t - (1-α_t)/√(1-α̅_t) · εθ(x_t, t))
  x_{t-1} = mean + σ_t · z
return x_0

docs.title: C3.3 Flow matching: ODE sampling by Heun (improved Euler)
docs.text:
set τ_0 = 0 < τ_1 < … < τ_S = 1
initialize x ~ N(0, I) at t = 0
for s = 0, …, S-1:
  t = τ_s,  t_next = τ_{s+1},  h = t_next - t
  k1 = vθ(x, t)
  x_pred = x + h · k1
  k2 = vθ(x_pred, t_next)
  x = x + (h/2) · (k1 + k2)
return x ≈ sample from p_data

docs.title: C4. Minimal PyTorch code snippets (training + sampling)
docs.text: These snippets are intentionally small and meant to make the variable ↔ formula correspondence explicit. For generic ODE/SDE solvers, see mathematics-foundation.md.

docs.title: C4.1 Score-based diffusion (VE/VP schedules + DSM loss + PC sampler)
docs.text:
import torch


def ve_marginal_std(t, *, sigma_min=0.01, sigma_max=50.0):
    """
    VE schedule: choose a marginal std σ(t) (not the diffusion coefficient g(t)).
    t: shape (B,) in [0,1].
    """
    return sigma_min * (sigma_max / sigma_min) ** t


def vp_beta(t, *, beta_min=0.1, beta_max=20.0):
    """VP noise rate β(t), t in [0,1]."""
    return beta_min + t * (beta_max - beta_min)


def vp_alpha_bar(t, *, beta_min=0.1, beta_max=20.0):
    """
    α̅(t) = exp(-∫_0^t β(s) ds) for linear β(s).
    """
    integral = beta_min * t + 0.5 * (beta_max - beta_min) * t * t
    return torch.exp(-integral)


def dsm_loss_ve(score_model, x0, t, *, sigma_min=0.01, sigma_max=50.0, weight=None):
    """
    VE denoising score matching:
      x_t = x0 + σ(t) ε
      ∇_{x_t} log p(x_t|x0) = -(x_t-x0)/σ(t)^2 = -ε/σ(t)
    """
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    sigma = ve_marginal_std(t, sigma_min=sigma_min, sigma_max=sigma_max)
    while sigma.ndim < x0.ndim:
        sigma = sigma[..., None]
    xt = x0 + sigma * eps
    target = -eps / sigma
    pred = score_model(xt, t)
    loss = (pred - target).pow(2)
    if weight is not None:
        w = weight(t)
        while w.ndim < loss.ndim:
            w = w[..., None]
        loss = w * loss
    return loss.mean()


@torch.no_grad()
def langevin_corrector(score_model, x, t, *, snr=0.16, n_steps=1):
    """
    K steps of overdamped Langevin dynamics at fixed t.
    Heuristic step size chosen to keep a target SNR.
    """
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        grad = score_model(x, t)
        noise = torch.randn_like(x)

        grad_norm = torch.norm(grad.reshape(grad.shape[0], -1), dim=-1).mean()
        noise_norm = torch.norm(noise.reshape(noise.shape[0], -1), dim=-1).mean()
        step_size = (snr * noise_norm / (grad_norm + 1e-12)) ** 2 * 2.0

        x = x + step_size * grad + torch.sqrt(2.0 * step_size) * noise
    return x


@torch.no_grad()
def pc_sampler(
    score_model, shape, *, n_steps=1000, sde="ve", device="cpu",
    corrector_steps=1, snr=0.16, sigma_min=0.01, sigma_max=50.0,
    beta_min=0.1, beta_max=20.0,
):
    """
    Predictor–corrector sampling.
    - VE predictor uses the identity g(t)^2 dt = d(σ(t)^2) for the chosen marginal σ(t).
    - VP predictor uses Euler–Maruyama with f(x,t)=-0.5β(t)x, g(t)=sqrt(β(t)).
    """
    if sde not in {"ve", "vp"}:
        raise ValueError("sde must be 've' or 'vp'")
    if n_steps < 2:
        raise ValueError("n_steps must include at least two time-grid points")
    x = torch.randn(shape, device=device)
    if sde == "ve":
        x = sigma_max * x  # terminal VE prior; match the training schedule
    ts = torch.linspace(1.0, 1e-3, n_steps, device=device)  # reverse-time grid

    for i in range(len(ts) - 1):
        t = ts[i].expand(shape[0])
        t_next = ts[i + 1].expand(shape[0])
        dt = t_next - t  # negative

        z = torch.randn_like(x)

        if sde == "ve":
            sigma = ve_marginal_std(t, sigma_min=sigma_min, sigma_max=sigma_max)
            sigma_next = ve_marginal_std(t_next, sigma_min=sigma_min, sigma_max=sigma_max)
            while sigma.ndim < x.ndim:
                sigma = sigma[..., None]
                sigma_next = sigma_next[..., None]
            d_sigma2 = sigma_next**2 - sigma**2  # negative
            x = x - d_sigma2 * score_model(x, t) + torch.sqrt(torch.clamp(-d_sigma2, min=0.0)) * z

        elif sde == "vp":
            beta = vp_beta(t, beta_min=beta_min, beta_max=beta_max)
            while beta.ndim < x.ndim:
                beta = beta[..., None]
            f = -0.5 * beta * x
            g = torch.sqrt(beta)
            dt_b = dt
            while dt_b.ndim < x.ndim:
                dt_b = dt_b[..., None]
            x = x + (f - (g**2) * score_model(x, t)) * dt_b + g * torch.sqrt(-dt_b) * z

        else:
            raise ValueError("sde must be 've' or 'vp'")

        x = langevin_corrector(score_model, x, t_next, snr=snr, n_steps=corrector_steps)

    return x

Correction (2026-10-14). The previous sampler initialized both VE and VP with standard Gaussian noise. For the default VE schedule, \(\sigma(1)=50\), so its approximate terminal prior has covariance \(2500I\), rather than \(I\). The VE branch now scales the initial noise and uses the same schedule parameters in its predictor; VP retains standard Gaussian initialization. These terminal priors are approximations to the finite-time noised data laws. With \(\sigma_{\min}>0\) and a positive stopping time, VE returns a slightly smoothed data law rather than an exact noiseless endpoint. Schedule arguments must match training. This agrees with the prior distinction in the official score-SDE implementation.

docs.title: C4.2 DDPM (noise-prediction training + ancestral sampler)
docs.text:
import torch


def ddpm_forward_sample(x0, t, alpha_bar):
    """
    x_t = sqrt(alpha_bar[t]) x0 + sqrt(1-alpha_bar[t]) eps
    alpha_bar: shape (T+1,) with alpha_bar[0]=1.
    t: int64 tensor of shape (B,) with values in {1,...,T}.
    """
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    a_bar = alpha_bar[t]
    while a_bar.ndim < x0.ndim:
        a_bar = a_bar[..., None]
    xt = torch.sqrt(a_bar) * x0 + torch.sqrt(1.0 - a_bar) * eps
    return xt, eps


def ddpm_loss_eps(eps_model, x0, t, alpha_bar):
    xt, eps = ddpm_forward_sample(x0, t, alpha_bar)
    pred_eps = eps_model(xt, t)
    return (pred_eps - eps).pow(2).mean()


@torch.no_grad()
def ddpm_sample(eps_model, shape, *, alpha, alpha_bar, sigma):
    """
    Ancestral sampling for a fixed-variance DDPM parameterization.
    Arrays alpha/alpha_bar/sigma are shape (T+1,) with index 0 unused for sampling.
    """
    device = alpha.device
    T = alpha.shape[0] - 1
    x = torch.randn(shape, device=device)

    for t in range(T, 0, -1):
        t_vec = torch.full((shape[0],), t, device=device, dtype=torch.long)
        eps = eps_model(x, t_vec)

        mean = (1.0 / torch.sqrt(alpha[t])) * (x - ((1.0 - alpha[t]) / torch.sqrt(1.0 - alpha_bar[t])) * eps)

        if t > 1:
            x = mean + sigma[t] * torch.randn_like(x)
        else:
            x = mean

    return x

docs.title: C4.3 Flow matching (linear bridge + ODE sampling)
docs.text:
import torch


def flow_matching_loss(v_model, x1, t):
    """
    Linear bridge between x0 ~ N(0,I) and x1 ~ data:
      x_t = (1-t) x0 + t x1
      target = d/dt x_t = x1 - x0
    """
    x0 = torch.randn_like(x1)
    t_for_path = t
    while t_for_path.ndim < x1.ndim:
        t_for_path = t_for_path[..., None]
    xt = (1.0 - t_for_path) * x0 + t_for_path * x1
    target = x1 - x0
    pred = v_model(xt, t)  # convention: model expects t with shape (B,)
    return (pred - target).pow(2).mean()


@torch.no_grad()
def flow_sample(v_model, shape, *, n_steps=50, method="heun", device="cpu"):
    """Sample by integrating dx/dt = v_model(x,t) from t=0 to t=1."""
    x = torch.randn(shape, device=device)
    ts = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, n_steps + 1, device=device)

    for i in range(n_steps):
        t = float(ts[i].item())
        t_next = float(ts[i + 1].item())
        h = t_next - t

        t_vec = torch.full((shape[0],), t, device=device)
        if method == "euler":
            x = x + h * v_model(x, t_vec)

        elif method == "heun":
            k1 = v_model(x, t_vec)
            x_pred = x + h * k1
            t_next_vec = torch.full((shape[0],), t_next, device=device)
            k2 = v_model(x_pred, t_next_vec)
            x = x + 0.5 * h * (k1 + k2)

        else:
            raise ValueError("method must be 'euler' or 'heun'")

    return x

docs.title: C5. ELBO policy (keep it light)
docs.text:
DDPM was originally introduced via a variational bound (an ELBO over a latent diffusion chain), but most practical training uses a simplified regression loss (e.g., noise prediction MSE) that can be derived as a special case of that ELBO under common parameterizations and fixed variances.

For details, see introduction-beta-CFM-and-ELBO.md and diffusion-models-intro.md (Chapter 4).

docs.title: C6. Section close template
docs.text:
1. We model: pick a view (score / noise / velocity).
  2. We learn: the corresponding network output (\(s_\theta\) / \(\varepsilon_\theta\) / \(v_\theta\)).
  3. We sample: the matching dynamics + numerical method (reverse SDE / reverse chain / ODE solver).

docs.title: Clarification (what this note is—and is not—claiming)
docs.text:
This note puts Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) and variational objectives (ELBO) side by side for a very specific reason: when designing a computable loss, both frameworks face a similar-looking obstacle—some marginal object is intractable, and we introduce conditional structure (auxiliary variables, conditional distributions, conditional expectations) to turn the optimization into an expectation we can sample or estimate.

However, this is a methodological similarity, not a semantic or “physical” equivalence. The objectives live on different mathematical objects:

  • ELBO is a variational lower bound on a log-marginal likelihood \(\log p_\theta(x)=\log\int p_\theta(x,z)\,dz\). Its construction is inseparable from Jensen’s inequality and an explicit inference distribution \(q_\phi(z\mid x)\).
  • Flow Matching / CFM is a path-matching / generator-regression viewpoint: we prescribe a probability path \((p_t)\) and learn a velocity field along that path. The intractable marginal target (e.g., a marginal velocity defined via posterior averaging) is replaced by a tractable conditional supervision signal, and the correctness of this replacement is justified by precise statements such as marginalization identities and gradient equivalence under Bregman losses.

So the purpose of this note is not to “derive Flow Matching from ELBO” (or vice versa), but to clarify:

  1. where the analogy does hold (turning intractable marginals into computable conditional objectives), and
  2. where it breaks (what is being optimized, what assumptions are required, and what guarantees we get).

With that scope fixed, we now recap the two optimization stories.

docs.title: Mathematics Foundation
docs.text: All discussions are in the Euclidean setting unless stated otherwise: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^D\), \(t\in[0,1]\). The goal is to pin down the minimum deterministic/stochastic differential-equation facts needed for flow models and diffusion models.

docs.title: Chapter 1 — Differential Equations (DE): first-order ODE / SDE
1.1 Foundation of Ordinary Differential Equations
docs.text:
Let \(u:[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^D\to\mathbb{R}^D\) be a time-dependent vector field. Consider the initial value problem (IVP)

\[ \frac{d}{dt}x(t)=u(t,x(t)),\qquad x(0)=x_0\in\mathbb{R}^D. \]

A standard sufficient condition for (global) existence and uniqueness on \([0,1]\) is:

  • \(u(t,x)\) is measurable in \(t\) and continuous in \(x\);
  • there is a nonnegative \(L\in L^1([0,1])\) such that \(\lVert u(t,x)-u(t,y)\rVert\le L(t)\lVert x-y\rVert\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^D\) and almost every \(t\); and
  • \(\lVert u(t,0)\rVert\le a(t)\) for a nonnegative \(a\in L^1([0,1])\), which gives the integrable growth bound \(\lVert u(t,x)\rVert\le a(t)+L(t)\lVert x\rVert\).

Under these Carathéodory conditions, solutions are absolutely continuous and satisfy the ODE almost everywhere. Joint continuity of \(u\) in \((t,x)\) gives the usual classical solution. The earlier statement omitted the time-measurability and integrable Lipschitz-bound requirements.

We write the solution as \(x(t;x_0)\) and define the flow map

\[ \psi_t(x_0):=x(t;x_0),\qquad \psi_0(x_0)=x_0. \]

One immediate consequence of uniqueness (hence of the Lipschitz-type assumptions above) is non-intersection of solution trajectories: if two solutions \(x_1(\cdot),x_2(\cdot)\) satisfy \(x_1(t_\ast)=x_2(t_\ast)\) at some time \(t_\ast\), then they must coincide for all \(t\) in their common interval of existence. (Proof sketch: treat \((t_\ast,x_1(t_\ast))\) as a new initial condition and apply uniqueness.)

docs.title: 1.1.1 Exponential integration factors (integration factor method)
docs.text:
This subsection is mainly about how to solve first-order ODEs in the cases where closed forms exist, and how to rewrite them into a form that is more structured (and numerically stable) when they do not.

Baseline. For a general nonlinear ODE \(\dot x=u(t,x)\), a closed form is usually unavailable; the “solution operator” is the flow map \(\psi_t\). In special cases, \(\psi_t\) can be written explicitly.

(A) Linear scalar ODE (homogeneous). Consider

\[ \frac{d}{dt}x(t)=L(t)\,x(t), \]

where \(L:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous. Then for any \(0\le s\le t\le 1\),

\[ x(t)=x(s)\,\exp\!\Big(\int_s^t L(\tau)\,d\tau\Big). \]

This motivates the exponential (integration) factor

\[ E(s\to t):=\exp\!\Big(\int_s^t L(\tau)\,d\tau\Big), \]

which accumulates the time-dependent linear effect.

(B) Linear scalar ODE (inhomogeneous): integrating factor. For

\[ \frac{d}{dt}x(t)=L(t)\,x(t)+r(t), \]

define \(E(s\to t)\) as above. Then the closed-form solution is

\[ x(t)=E(s\to t)\,x(s)+\int_s^t E(\tau\to t)\,r(\tau)\,d\tau. \]

This is the standard integrating-factor method.

(C) Semilinear ODE: variation of constants / Duhamel formula. More generally, consider a semilinear ODE

\[ \frac{d}{dt}x(t)=L(t)\,x(t)+N(x(t),t), \]

where \(x(t)\in\mathbb{R}^D\), \(L(t)\in\mathbb{R}\) (equivalently \(L(t)I\) acting on \(\mathbb{R}^D\)), and \(N:\mathbb{R}^D\times[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^D\). Multiplying by \(E(s\to t)^{-1}\) and applying the product rule yields

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\Big[E(s\to t)^{-1}x(t)\Big]=E(s\to t)^{-1}N(x(t),t). \]

Integrating from \(s\) to \(t\) gives the integral form (Duhamel / variation-of-constants formula)

\[ x(t)=E(s\to t)\,x(s)\;+\;\int_s^t E(\tau\to t)\,N(x(\tau),\tau)\,d\tau. \]

This separates the evolution into a closed-form linear propagation and a nonlinear residual. Exponential integrators discretize only the integral term while handling the linear propagation exactly, often improving stability when the linear part is stiff.

Remark (matrix-valued linear part). If the linear part is \(L(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}\), the same integral formula holds with \(E(s\to t)\) defined as the fundamental matrix solving \(\frac{d}{dt}E(s\to t)=L(t)E(s\to t)\), \(E(s\to s)=I\). In general \(E(s\to t)\neq \exp\!\big(\int_s^t L(\tau)\,d\tau\big)\) unless \(L(t)\) commutes with itself at different times (or \(L\) is constant).

What is “closed form” here (and when do we still need numerics)? For a generic nonlinear first-order ODE, a closed-form solution is not available. Case (A) is fully explicit. Case (B) is explicit up to quadrature: if the integral \(\int_s^t E(\tau\to t)r(\tau)\,d\tau\) can be evaluated analytically then we obtain a closed form; otherwise we still compute that integral numerically. Case (C) provides an exact integral representation, but since \(N\) depends on the unknown trajectory \(x(\tau)\), it is generally an implicit integral equation and still requires numerical approximation (e.g., time stepping, Picard iteration, or exponential integrators).

Diffeomorphism is about regularity/invertibility, not linearity. In flow models, we often care that the time-\(t\) map \(\psi_t\) is a (local) \(C^1\) diffeomorphism so that the transformation is invertible and change-of-variables identities make sense. This property does not require the dynamics to be linear. Rather, it follows from ODE well-posedness plus smoothness: if \(u(t,\cdot)\) is (locally) Lipschitz (uniqueness) and \(C^1\) in \(x\) on a domain where solutions exist up to time \(t\), then \(\psi_t\) is (locally) invertible and differentiable, with inverse given by running the same ODE backward in time. Nonlinearity is typical and compatible with diffeomorphism; linearity is only a special case where we may also get closed-form expressions.

docs.title: 1.1.2 Numerical solvers for ODEs (time discretization)
docs.text:
Closed-form solutions are rare for nonlinear, time-dependent ODEs, so we typically approximate trajectories numerically. A useful starting point is the integral form of the ODE

\[ \dot x(t)=v(x(t),t),\qquad x(0)=x_0, \]

namely

\[ x(t)=x_0+\int_0^t v(x(\tau),\tau)\,d\tau. \]

Numerical solvers discretize time and approximate this integral by evaluating the vector field \(v\) at selected points.

Discretization. Choose grid points \(0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_N=T\) with step sizes \(h_n:=t_{n+1}-t_n\), and maintain states \(x_n\approx x(t_n)\).

Order of accuracy (one line). A method is called order-\(p\) if, for a sufficiently smooth solution and a uniform step size \(h\), its global error at \(T\) scales as \(O(h^p)\) as \(h\to 0\) (equivalently, local truncation error \(O(h^{p+1})\)).

Euler (explicit). The simplest one-step method uses the current slope:

\[ x_{n+1}=x_n+h_n\,v(x_n,t_n). \]

It is first-order accurate: local truncation error \(O(h_n^2)\) and global error \(O(\max_n h_n)\) under standard regularity assumptions.

Heun (improved Euler / explicit trapezoid). A second-order predictor–corrector:

\[ \tilde x_{n+1}=x_n+h_n\,v(x_n,t_n),\qquad x_{n+1}=x_n+\frac{h_n}{2}\Big(v(x_n,t_n)+v(\tilde x_{n+1},t_{n+1})\Big). \]

It has local error \(O(h_n^3)\) and global error \(O((\max_n h_n)^2)\).

Runge–Kutta (RK4). A standard fourth-order method based on four slopes:

\[ k_1=v(x_n,t_n),\quad k_2=v\Big(x_n+\frac{h_n}{2}k_1,t_n+\frac{h_n}{2}\Big),\quad k_3=v\Big(x_n+\frac{h_n}{2}k_2,t_n+\frac{h_n}{2}\Big),\quad k_4=v(x_n+h_n k_3,t_n+h_n), \] \[ x_{n+1}=x_n+\frac{h_n}{6}\big(k_1+2k_2+2k_3+k_4\big). \]

RK4 is a common accuracy–cost tradeoff when vector-field evaluations are not too expensive.

Semilinear structure and exponential integrators. If \(v(x,t)=L(t)x+N(x,t)\) (Section 1.1.1), then

\[ x(t)=E(0\to t)x_0+\int_0^t E(\tau\to t)\,N(x(\tau),\tau)\,d\tau, \]

and exponential integrators approximate only the integral term while handling the linear propagation \(E(\cdot\to\cdot)\) analytically. This can substantially improve stability when the linear part is stiff.

Reverse-time integration (ODE). Solving backward from a terminal condition \(x(T)=x_T\) is straightforward: integrate on a decreasing grid \(t_0=T>t_1>\dots>t_N=0\). With Euler and constant step \(h>0\),

\[ t_{n+1}=t_n-h,\qquad x_{n+1}=x_n-h\,v(x_n,t_n). \]

For ODEs, this is just a reparameterization of time; in diffusion models, reverse-time ODE integration is used for sampling (e.g., probability flow ODEs).

Remark (stability and stiffness). For stiff dynamics, explicit methods may require very small step sizes for stability; implicit methods or structure-exploiting solvers (e.g., exponential integrators, diffusion-specific solvers) can be preferable.

Minimal code (Euler / Heun / RK4). Below is a tiny reference implementation for the scalar ODE \( \dot x=v(x,t) \). The same structure applies to \(x\in\mathbb{R}^D\) by letting x be a NumPy/PyTorch array/tensor and having v(x,t) return the same shape.

from typing import Callable, Literal, Tuple, List

Method = Literal["euler", "heun", "rk4"]


def solve_ode(
    v: Callable[[float, float], float],
    x0: float,
    t0: float,
    t1: float,
    n_steps: int,
    method: Method = "euler",
) -> Tuple[List[float], List[float]]:
    """
    Solve dx/dt = v(x,t) on [t0,t1] with a chosen explicit solver.
    - method: "euler" | "heun" | "rk4"
    """
    if n_steps <= 0:
        raise ValueError("n_steps must be positive")

    h = (t1 - t0) / n_steps
    t = t0
    x = x0
    ts = [t]
    xs = [x]

    for _ in range(n_steps):
        if method == "euler":
            x = x + h * v(x, t)

        elif method == "heun":
            k1 = v(x, t)
            x_pred = x + h * k1
            k2 = v(x_pred, t + h)
            x = x + (h / 2.0) * (k1 + k2)

        elif method == "rk4":
            k1 = v(x, t)
            k2 = v(x + 0.5 * h * k1, t + 0.5 * h)
            k3 = v(x + 0.5 * h * k2, t + 0.5 * h)
            k4 = v(x + h * k3, t + h)
            x = x + (h / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)

        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown method: {method}")

        t = t + h
        ts.append(t)
        xs.append(x)

    return ts, xs

docs.title: 1.2 Random initial condition (random IVP)
docs.text:
Fix a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\). Let \(\mathbf{X}_0:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^D\) be an \(\mathcal{F}\)-measurable random variable with law \(\mu_0:=\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_0)\). Define

\[ \mathbf{X}_t:=\psi_t(\mathbf{X}_0),\qquad t\in[0,1], \]

and denote \(\mu_t:=\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X}_t)\). This is still a deterministic ODE; randomness enters only through \(\mathbf{X}_0\).

docs.title: 1.3 Push-forward of measures and test-function identity
docs.text:
For each \(t\), the law evolves by push-forward:

\[ \mu_t = (\psi_t)_\#\mu_0. \]

Equivalently, for any bounded measurable \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^D\to\mathbb{R}\),

\[ \mathbb{E}\big[\varphi(\mathbf{X}_t)\big] = \int_{\mathbb{R}^D}\varphi(\psi_t(x))\,\mu_0(dx). \]

docs.title: 1.4 Foundation of Stochastic Differential Equations
docs.text: This section provides an intuition-first bridge from ODEs to SDEs. Chapter 2 then states the Itô SDE and the associated density evolution (Fokker–Planck).

docs.title: 1.4.1 From ODEs to SDEs (discretization intuition)
docs.text:
Start from a deterministic ODE in \(\mathbb{R}^D\):

\[ \frac{d}{dt}x(t)=f(x(t),t),\qquad x(0)=x_0,\qquad t\in[0,T]. \]

Euler time stepping with step size \(\Delta t\) gives

\[ x_{t+\Delta t}\approx x_t+f(x_t,t)\,\Delta t. \]

To model uncertainty or unmodeled interactions, add a random perturbation at each time step:

\[ x_{t+\Delta t}\approx x_t+f(x_t,t)\,\Delta t+g(t)\,\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_D)\ \text{i.i.d.} \]

The \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) scaling is crucial: it is the scaling (up to constants) for which the cumulative randomness remains \(O(1)\) over \(O(1)\) time, rather than vanishing (\(\Delta t\)) or exploding (\(1\)).

In the continuous-time limit, this leads to an Itô SDE

\[ dX_t=f(X_t,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t, \]

where \(W_t\in\mathbb{R}^D\) is a standard Brownian motion (Wiener process) characterized by:

  • \(W_0=0\) a.s.;
  • independent increments: \(W_t-W_s\) is independent of \(\sigma(W_u:u\le s)\) for \(0\le s<t\);
  • Gaussian increments: \(W_t-W_s\sim \mathcal{N}(0,(t-s)I_D)\);
  • sample paths are a.s. continuous but nowhere classically differentiable.

The notation \(dW_t:=W_{t+dt}-W_t\) is a convenient shorthand for these increments and should not be interpreted as a classical differential. Informally, one writes

\[ dW_t\sim \mathcal{N}(0,dt\,I_D), \]

meaning that over a short interval of length \(dt\), the increment behaves like a zero-mean Gaussian with covariance \(dt\,I_D\).

docs.title: 1.4.2 How to read an Itô SDE: integral form and Itô integration intuition
docs.text:
An SDE should be understood through its integral formulation. For example, the Itô SDE

\[ dX_t=f(X_t,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t,\qquad X_0=x_0, \]

means that for each \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[ X_t = X_0 +\int_0^t f(X_s,s)\,ds +\int_0^t g(s)\,dW_s, \]

where the first integral is a classical (Lebesgue/Riemann) integral and the second is an Itô stochastic integral.

We do not build the Itô integral rigorously here; instead, keep the following intuition in mind. For a partition \(0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_N=t\), the Itô integral can be viewed (informally) as a limit of left-point Riemann sums:

\[ \int_0^t g(s)\,dW_s \approx \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} g(t_i)\,\big(W_{t_{i+1}}-W_{t_i}\big), \]

with convergence in probability (under suitable conditions). The left-endpoint evaluation \(g(t_i)\) is what distinguishes the Itô convention from other conventions (e.g., Stratonovich often corresponds to midpoint-type evaluations).

Because Brownian sample paths are a.s. continuous but nowhere classically differentiable, expressions like \(dW_t/dt\) do not exist in the usual sense, and classical “integrate both sides” reasoning does not apply directly. The differential notation \(dX_t\), \(dt\), \(dW_t\) is therefore shorthand for increments and must be interpreted through the integral equation above.

Comparison with ODEs. For an ODE \(\dot x(t)=f(x(t),t)\), the integral form

\[ x(t)=x(0)+\int_0^t f(x(\tau),\tau)\,d\tau \]

is justified by the fundamental theorem of calculus (differentiability recovers the function from its derivative). For SDEs, there is no direct analog because \(W_t\) is not differentiable and stochastic integrals do not obey the classical chain rule. Instead, the correct replacement is Itô’s formula (Itô’s lemma), which we will use later when connecting SDEs to density evolution and reverse-time constructions in diffusion models.

Minimal code (Euler–Maruyama / Milstein). The most common time stepping for Itô SDEs is Euler–Maruyama. Below is a small reference implementation for

\[ dX_t=f(X_t,t)\,dt+G(X_t,t)\,dW_t, \]

where \(W_t\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(G(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times m}\). Milstein is included only for the scalar case \(D=m=1\).

from typing import Callable, Literal, Tuple, Optional

import numpy as np

SdeMethod = Literal["euler_maruyama", "milstein_scalar"]


def solve_sde(
    f: Callable[[np.ndarray, float], np.ndarray],
    G: Callable[[np.ndarray, float], np.ndarray],
    x0,
    t0: float,
    t1: float,
    n_steps: int,
    *,
    method: SdeMethod = "euler_maruyama",
    rng: Optional[np.random.Generator] = None,
    dgdx_scalar: Optional[Callable[[float, float], float]] = None,
) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """
    Solve the Itô SDE: dX = f(X,t) dt + G(X,t) dW, with W in R^m.

    - f(x,t): (D,) -> (D,)
    - G(x,t): (D,) -> (D,m)
    - x0: float or array-like of shape (D,)
    - method:
        - "euler_maruyama": works for any (D,m)
        - "milstein_scalar": only for D=m=1; requires dgdx_scalar(x,t)=d/dx g(x,t)
          where G(x,t) = [[g(x,t)]].
    """
    if n_steps <= 0:
        raise ValueError("n_steps must be positive")
    if t1 <= t0:
        raise ValueError("require t1 > t0 for this forward-time solver")

    rng = np.random.default_rng() if rng is None else rng

    x = np.asarray(x0, dtype=float)
    if x.ndim == 0:
        x = x.reshape((1,))

    t = float(t0)
    h = (t1 - t0) / n_steps

    ts = np.empty(n_steps + 1, dtype=float)
    xs = np.empty((n_steps + 1,) + x.shape, dtype=float)
    ts[0] = t
    xs[0] = x

    for n in range(n_steps):
        drift = np.asarray(f(x, t), dtype=float).reshape(x.shape)
        diffusion = np.asarray(G(x, t), dtype=float)
        if diffusion.ndim != 2:
            raise ValueError("G(x,t) must return a 2D array of shape (D,m)")
        D, m = diffusion.shape
        if D != x.shape[0]:
            raise ValueError("G(x,t) first dimension must match x dimension D")

        dW = rng.standard_normal(size=(m,)) * np.sqrt(h)  # N(0, h I_m)

        if method == "euler_maruyama":
            x = x + h * drift + diffusion @ dW

        elif method == "milstein_scalar":
            if not (D == 1 and m == 1 and x.shape == (1,)):
                raise ValueError("milstein_scalar requires D=m=1 and scalar state")
            if dgdx_scalar is None:
                raise ValueError("milstein_scalar requires dgdx_scalar")
            g = float(diffusion[0, 0])
            gp = float(dgdx_scalar(float(x[0]), t))
            x = x + h * drift + diffusion @ dW + 0.5 * g * gp * (dW[0] ** 2 - h)

        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown method: {method}")

        t = t + h
        ts[n + 1] = t
        xs[n + 1] = x

    return ts, xs

docs.title: Chapter 2 — Density Evolution: From change of variables to Fokker–Planck
docs.text:
This chapter summarizes the two canonical density-evolution PDEs:

  • deterministic transport (ODE) \(\Rightarrow\) continuity equation;
  • stochastic diffusion (Itô SDE) \(\Rightarrow\) Fokker–Planck equation.

docs.title: 2.1 Change-of-Variable Formula: From Deterministic Maps to Stochastic Flows
docs.text: This section starts from a single deterministic update \(x_1=\Psi(x_0)\) and tracks how densities transform under smooth bijections. Composing many such updates leads to the Jacobian-determinant bookkeeping used in normalizing flows. Taking a continuous-time limit recovers the continuity equation; adding Brownian noise upgrades it to the Fokker–Planck equation (Section 2.2).

docs.title: 2.1.1 Single deterministic map
docs.text:
Let \(\Psi:\mathbb{R}^D o\mathbb{R}^D\) be a \(C^1\) bijection with \(C^1\) inverse (a diffeomorphism). If \(X_0\sim p_0\) and \(X_1:=\Psi(X_0)\), then \(X_1\sim p_1\) where the density is given by the change-of-variable formula

\[ p_1(x_1)=p_0 ig(\Psi^{-1}(x_1) ig)\,\left|\det abla \Psi^{-1}(x_1) ight|. \]

Equivalently, writing \(x_1=\Psi(x_0)\),

\[ p_0(x_0)=p_1(\Psi(x_0))\,\left|\det abla\Psi(x_0) ight|. \]

Interpretation: \(\left|\det abla\Psi ight|\) is the local volume change, and the density compensates to conserve probability mass.

At the measure level, this is exactly a push-forward:

\[ \mu_1 = \Psi_\#\mu_0, \]

meaning \(\mu_1(A)=\mu_0(\Psi^{-1}(A))\) for any Borel set \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^D\). The density formula above is the Lebesgue-density version of \(\mu_1=\Psi_\#\mu_0\).

As a special case, if \(\Psi(x)=Ax\) with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{D imes D}\) invertible, then

\[ p_1(x_1)=p_0(A^{-1}x_1)\,|\det A^{-1}|. \]

docs.title: 2.1.2 Composing multiple bijections (discrete normalizing flows)
docs.text:
Consider a sequence of diffeomorphisms \(\Psi_1,\dots,\Psi_L\) and states \(x_k=\Psi_k(x_{k-1})\). If \(X_0\sim p_0\), define \(X_k:=\Psi_k(X_{k-1})\) and let \(p_k\) be the density of \(X_k\). Mass conservation at each step implies

\[ p_k(x_k)=p_{k-1}(x_{k-1})\left|\det abla\Psi_k(x_{k-1}) ight|^{-1}, \qquad x_{k-1}=\Psi_k^{-1}(x_k). \]

Recursing yields the overall Jacobian product

\[ p_L(x_L)=p_0(x_0)\prod_{k=1}^L \left|\det abla\Psi_k(x_{k-1}) ight|^{-1}, \]

and, in log form,

\[ \log p_L(x_L)=\log p_0(x_0)-\sum_{k=1}^L \log\left|\det abla\Psi_k(x_{k-1}) ight|. \]

This is the core likelihood bookkeeping identity for (discrete) normalizing flows.

docs.title: 2.1.3 Continuous-time limit \(\Rightarrow\) continuity equation
docs.text:
Let \(u(t,x)\) be a time-dependent velocity field and consider the ODE \(\dot x(t)=u(t,x(t))\). A standard way to connect maps to flows is to take small steps

\[ \Psi_{t o t+\Delta t}(x)\approx x+u(t,x)\,\Delta t, \]

so the Jacobian factor becomes \(\det(I+\Delta t\, abla_x u(t,x))\). In the limit \(\Delta t o 0\), the density \(p_t\) (when it exists and is smooth enough) evolves according to the continuity equation

\[ \partial_t p_t(x)+ abla\!\cdot ig(p_t(x)\,u(t,x) ig)=0.\qquad ext{(CE)} \]

Along trajectories \(X_t\) solving the ODE, an equivalent form is

\[ rac{d}{dt}\log p_t(X_t)=- abla\!\cdot u(t,X_t). \]

Regularity of \(u\) \(\Rightarrow\) an invertible flow map. Under standard ODE well-posedness assumptions (e.g., \(u(t,\cdot)\) locally Lipschitz in \(x\) and sufficiently regular in \(t\)), for each initial condition \(x_0\) there is a unique trajectory \(t\mapsto x(t;x_0)\). This defines the time-\(t\) flow map

\[ \psi_t(x_0):=x(t;x_0). \]

Uniqueness implies non-intersection of trajectories, and in particular makes \(\psi_t\) (locally) invertible on its domain of existence: the inverse is given by running the same ODE backward in time, i.e., \(\psi_t^{-1}=\psi_{t o 0}\) whenever both flows are well-defined. If \(u\) is \(C^1\) in \(x\), then \(\psi_t\) is (locally) a \(C^1\) diffeomorphism.

Derivation sketch (via change of variables). View the ODE as the continuous-time limit of small bijective updates (forward Euler):

\[ x_{t+\Delta t}=\Psi(x_t):=x_t+\Delta t\,u(t,x_t). \]

Then

\[ abla_{x_t}\Psi(x_t)=I+\Delta t\, abla_x u(t,x_t)+O(\Delta t^2), \]

and hence

\[ \det( abla_{x_t}\Psi)=1+\Delta t\, abla\!\cdot u(t,x_t)+O(\Delta t^2), \]

using \(\det(I+\Delta t A)=1+\Delta t\,\mathrm{tr}(A)+O(\Delta t^2)\) and \( abla\!\cdot u=\mathrm{tr}( abla_x u)\). Applying the change-of-variable formula to the update gives

\[ \log p_{t+\Delta t}(x_{t+\Delta t})-\log p_t(x_t) = -\Delta t\, abla\!\cdot u(t,x_t)+O(\Delta t^2). \]

On the other hand, a Taylor expansion yields

\[ \log p_{t+\Delta t}(x_{t+\Delta t})-\log p_t(x_t) = \Delta t\,\partial_t\log p_t(x_t) +\Delta t\,u(t,x_t)^ op abla_x\log p_t(x_t) +O(\Delta t^2). \]

Matching \(O(\Delta t)\) terms and rewriting via the product rule recovers (CE) (and the trajectory form above).

At the measure level, the ODE flow map \(\psi_t\) (when well-defined) pushes the initial law forward:

\[ \mu_t = (\psi_t)_\#\mu_0. \]

When \(\mu_t(dx)=p_t(x)\,dx\) exists, the continuity equation (CE) is the density-level expression of \(\mu_t=(\psi_t)_\#\mu_0\).

docs.title: 2.1.4 ODE vs SDE: push-forward map vs stochastic evolution
docs.text:
For an Itô SDE, sample paths satisfy

\[ dX_t=b(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma(t,X_t)\,dW_t, \]

and \(X_t\) is no longer a deterministic function of \(X_0\). Consequently, in general there is no single deterministic map \(\psi_t\) such that \(\mu_t=(\psi_t)_\#\mu_0\).

Instead, the law evolves via a two-time Markov transition kernel \(P_{s,t}\), with \(0\le s\le t\le1\). Below write \(P_t:=P_{0,t}\) for evolution from the fixed initial time. For time-dependent coefficients this is a transition family, not generally a one-parameter semigroup; semigroup notation applies in the time-homogeneous case. In a notation that mirrors the push-forward \(\#\), it is common to view \(P_t\) as inducing a push-forward operator on measures (the adjoint of \(P_t\) acting on test functions).

Kernel \(\Rightarrow\) measure push-forward. Let \(P_t(x,\cdot)\) be a probability measure on \(\mathbb{R}^D\) for each \(x\), and write \(P_t(x,A)\) for its mass on a Borel set \(A\). Define the induced operator \(P_t^\ast\) on measures by

\[ (P_t^\ast \mu_0)(A) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} P_t(x,A)\,\mu_0(dx), \qquad A\ \text{Borel}. \]

Then the law evolution is simply

\[ \mu_t = P_t^\ast \mu_0. \]

Many notes also write this as \(\mu_t=\mu_0 P_t\) (right action) or, informally, \(\mu_t=(P_t)_\#\mu_0\) to emphasize “push-forward by a stochastic mechanism”. The safest (unambiguous) notation is \(P_t^\ast \mu_0\).

Dual (test-function) form. The same evolution can be written as

\[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^D}\varphi(x)\,\mu_t(dx) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} (P_t\varphi)(x)\,\mu_0(dx), \qquad (P_t\varphi)(x):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^D}\varphi(y)\,P_t(x,dy), \]

for bounded measurable \(\varphi\). This is exactly the “kernel vs measure” adjoint relationship: \(P_t\) acts on functions, \(P_t^\ast\) acts on measures.

Deterministic maps as a special case. If \(P_t\) comes from a deterministic map \(\psi_t\), then

\[ P_t(x,dy)=\delta_{\psi_t(x)}(dy) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P_t^\ast \mu_0 = (\psi_t)_\#\mu_0. \]

So the usual push-forward \((\psi_t)_\#\) is recovered by taking a Dirac transition kernel.

When a density \(p_t\) exists, this kernel-level evolution is described by the Fokker–Planck equation (Section 2.2), which differs from the continuity equation by a second-order diffusion term.

Velocity-first vs density-first (Eulerian vs Lagrangian). There is an important asymmetry:

  • Velocity-first: specifying \(u(t,\cdot)\) (under well-posedness assumptions) determines the flow map \(\psi_t\), hence determines the pushed-forward laws \(\mu_t=(\psi_t)_\#\mu_0\) and (when densities exist) a unique density evolution via (CE).
  • Density-first: specifying only a density path \(t\mapsto p_t\) generally does not determine a unique velocity field. Indeed, if a vector field \(w_t(x)\) satisfies
\[ \nabla\!\cdot\big(p_t(x)\,w_t(x)\big)=0, \]

then both \(u_t\) and \(u_t+w_t\) produce the same right-hand side in (CE), hence the same density evolution. A single density path may correspond to many different particle flows.

Realizability (consistency check). Not every arbitrary path \(p_t\) can arise as the marginal law of particles moving under some deterministic velocity field. The continuity equation provides a consistency condition: we say \(p_t\) is realizable (generated by a flow) if there exists \(u(t,x)\) such that \(p_t\) and \(u\) satisfy (CE) (with suitable boundary/decay conditions).

(Optional) Conditioning. If we introduce an auxiliary variable \(Z\sim\pi\) and define a conditional velocity field \(u(t,x\mid z)\), then for each fixed \(z\) we have a conditional push-forward and continuity equation:

\[ p_t(\cdot\mid z)=(\psi_t(\cdot;z))_\# p_0,\qquad \partial_t p_t(x\mid z)+\nabla\!\cdot\big(p_t(x\mid z)\,u(t,x\mid z)\big)=0. \]

The unconditional marginal is the mixture

\[ p_t(x)=\int p_t(x\mid z)\,\pi(z)\,dz. \]

docs.title: 2.1.5 Path-first (density-first) vs velocity-first: where diffusion and flow matching fit
docs.text:
In modern generative modeling, it is useful to separate two design patterns:

  • Path-first / density-first: first specify (explicitly or implicitly) a probability path \((\mu_t)_{t\in[0,1]}\) or a forward corruption mechanism that induces \(\mu_t\), and then learn dynamics that are consistent with that path.
  • Velocity-first: first specify a parameterized dynamics family (e.g., a flow map or vector field \(u_\theta\)), and then fit it to data using an objective; the induced path \(\mu_t\) is whatever that dynamics produces.

Flow-based generative modeling can be understood as a Lagrangian particle system whose Eulerian density evolution satisfies the continuity equation (in a suitable weak sense, and as a pointwise PDE under additional regularity), expressing pure transport and conservation of probability mass. This is a useful intuition for why, in a velocity-first viewpoint, we do not “impose (CE) as a constraint”: once we specify the particle dynamics \(\dot X_t=u(t,X_t)\) and define \(\mu_t=(\psi_t)_\#\mu_0\), (CE) follows as the density-level statement of mass conservation. By contrast, in a path-first/density-first viewpoint, (CE) acts as a compatibility condition between a prescribed \(p_t\) and a velocity field \(u\).

Here “first” refers to what is treated as the design input in modeling/derivation/training (what you specify up front), not what is “known during sampling”. In both paradigms, once dynamics are learned, sampling proceeds by integrating an ODE/SDE.

“Design input” means something you choose to specify that defines the modeling problem; “known” means something that is already given at a particular stage of an algorithm/derivation (often as an output of a previous stage).

Diffusion models and flow matching are typically path-first:

  • Diffusion models: choose a forward noising SDE (equivalently a noise schedule such as \(\beta(t)\) or \(\alpha(t),\sigma(t)\)), which defines a tractable forward path that “thickens” the data distribution. Training then learns a reverse-time object (often the score) that makes sampling possible.
  • Flow matching / CFM: choose a probability path via a coupling + interpolation (e.g., endpoint pairing and \(\gamma_t(x_0,x_1)\)), then learn a velocity field that generates (or matches) that path.

In this path-first viewpoint, the continuity equation (CE) plays the role of a consistency condition: a velocity field \(u\) generates a density path \(p_t\) only if \(p_t\) and \(u\) satisfy (CE). In practice we rarely “solve (CE) for \(u\)” directly because \(p_t\) is not available in closed form; instead, training objectives are designed as computable surrogates that guarantee (or approximate) the same consistency.

Finally, note that sampling is always velocity-first in execution: once a model provides a drift/velocity (ODE or SDE), we generate samples by numerically integrating the learned dynamics.

docs.title: 2.2 Stochastic dynamics: Itô SDE
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{W}_t\) be a standard \(m\)-dimensional Brownian motion. Consider the Itô SDE

\[ d\mathbf{X}_t = b(t,\mathbf{X}_t)\,dt + \sigma(t,\mathbf{X}_t)\,d\mathbf{W}_t, \]

where \(b:[0,1] imes\mathbb{R}^D o\mathbb{R}^D\) is the drift and \(\sigma:[0,1] imes\mathbb{R}^D o\mathbb{R}^{D imes m}\) is the diffusion coefficient. Define the diffusion matrix

\[ a(t,x):=\sigma(t,x)\sigma(t,x)^ op\in\mathbb{R}^{D imes D}. \]

Assume \(\mu_t(dx)=p_t(x)\,dx\) exists and \(b,\sigma\) are regular enough. Then \(p_t\) satisfies the Fokker–Planck (forward Kolmogorov) equation

\[ \partial_t p_t(x) = - abla\!\cdot ig(b(t,x)\,p_t(x) ig) \;+\; rac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^D\sum_{j=1}^D \partial_{x_i}\partial_{x_j}\! ig(a_{ij}(t,x)\,p_t(x) ig). \]

Special cases:

  • Pure transport (\(\sigma\equiv 0\)): the second-order term vanishes and we recover the continuity equation.
  • Isotropic diffusion (\(a(t,x)= eta(t)I\)): the second-order term becomes \( rac{1}{2} eta(t)\Delta p_t\).

In the diffusion-model setting, a common special case is

\[ dX_t=f(X_t,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t,\qquad W_t\in\mathbb{R}^D, \]

i.e., \(\sigma(t,x)=g(t)I\). Then

\[ \partial_t p_t(x) = - abla\!\cdot ig(f(x,t)\,p_t(x) ig) \;+\; rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\,\Delta p_t(x). \]

Using \( abla p_t=p_t abla\log p_t\), this can be rewritten in a divergence (mass conservation) form:

\[ \partial_t p_t(x) = - abla\!\cdot\Big(\Big(f(x,t)- rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\, abla_x\log p_t(x)\Big)\,p_t(x)\Big). \]

Here the first term transports probability mass by the drift, while the Laplacian term models spreading (diffusion) due to stochastic noise. A full derivation uses Itô calculus and is omitted here.

docs.title: 2.3 Intuition of the Continuity Equation
docs.text: The continuity equation is a conservation law for a density. In our context, it describes conservation of probability mass under deterministic transport.

docs.title: 2.3.1 Physical interpretation (control volume and flux)
docs.text:
Think of a small fixed box (control volume) whose lower corner is \(\xi=(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3\), with side lengths \(\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z\). Let \(p(\xi,t)\) be the density of a conserved quantity (mass or probability). The total amount inside the box is approximately

\[ p(\xi,t)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z. \]

Changes can only happen via flux across the boundary. Let \(j(\xi,t)\in\mathbb{R}^3\) be the flux vector (amount crossing unit area per unit time). The net outflux in the \(x\)-direction is approximately

\[ ig(j_x(x+\Delta x,y,z,t)-j_x(x,y,z,t) ig)\,\Delta y\,\Delta z, \]

and similarly for the other directions. Summing the three directions, the total net outflux is

\[ +\,( abla\!\cdot j)(\xi,t)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z. \]

Conservation says “rate of change inside = minus net outflux”, hence

\[ \partial_t p(\xi,t)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z = -\,( abla\!\cdot j)(\xi,t)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z. \]

Canceling the volume factor (valid for any sufficiently small box) yields the local form

\[ \partial_t p(\xi,t)+ abla\!\cdot j(\xi,t)=0. \]

For deterministic particle transport with velocity field \(u(x,t)\), the natural flux is \(j=p\,u\). Plugging this into the conservation law gives the continuity equation

\[ \partial_t p+ abla\!\cdot(p\,u)=0, \]

which is exactly (CE) in Section 2.1.3.

Correction (2026-10-14). The earlier face-difference and total-outflux expressions had the sign of net influx, while the final continuity equation had the correct sign. Outflux is the right-face contribution minus the left-face contribution; accumulation is its negative. For example, positive divergence gives net outward flow and decreases the amount in a fixed box.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Derivation from a global conservation law (divergence theorem)
docs.text:
Let \(p(x,t)\) be a density on \(\mathbb{R}^D\), \(u(x,t)\) a velocity field, and \(V\subset\mathbb{R}^D\) an arbitrary control volume with boundary \(\partial V\) and outward unit normal \(n\). The total mass in \(V\) is

\[ \int_V p(x,t)\,dx, \]

so its time derivative is the accumulation rate \( rac{d}{dt}\int_V p\,dx\). The outward flux through the boundary is

\[ \int_{\partial V} p(x,t)\,u(x,t)\cdot n(x)\,dS. \]

Conservation requires

\[ rac{d}{dt}\int_V p\,dx+\int_{\partial V} p\,u\cdot n\,dS=0. \]

Using the divergence theorem,

\[ \int_{\partial V} p\,u\cdot n\,dS=\int_V abla\!\cdot(p\,u)\,dx, \]

so

\[ \int_V ig(\partial_t p+ abla\!\cdot(p\,u) ig)\,dx=0. \]

Since \(V\) is arbitrary, the integrand must vanish (in the weak sense), yielding

\[ \partial_t p+ abla\!\cdot(p\,u)=0. \]

docs.title: Appendix A — Integrating factor derivation (scalar linear ODE)
docs.text: This appendix spells out the algebra behind the integrating-factor identity used in Section 1.1.1.

docs.title: A.1 Problem
docs.text:
Let \(L:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(r:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuous. Consider the inhomogeneous linear ODE

\[ \dot x(t)=L(t)x(t)+r(t),\qquad t\in[0,1]. \]

Fix \(0\le s\le t\le 1\) and assume \(x(\cdot)\) is differentiable.

docs.title: A.2 Step 1: define the integration factor and its derivative
docs.text:
Define

\[ E(s\to t):=\exp\!\Big(\int_s^t L(\tau)\,d\tau\Big), \qquad E^{-1}(s\to t):=\exp\!\Big(-\int_s^t L(\tau)\,d\tau\Big). \]

By the chain rule and the fundamental theorem of calculus,

\[ \frac{d}{dt}E^{-1}(s\to t) = E^{-1}(s\to t)\cdot\frac{d}{dt}\Big(-\int_s^t L(\tau)\,d\tau\Big) = -L(t)\,E^{-1}(s\to t). \]

docs.title: A.3 Step 2: product rule (the key identity)
docs.text:
Using the product rule,

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\Big(E^{-1}(s\to t)x(t)\Big) = \Big(\frac{d}{dt}E^{-1}(s\to t)\Big)x(t)+E^{-1}(s\to t)\dot x(t). \]

Substituting \(\frac{d}{dt}E^{-1}(s\to t)=-L(t)E^{-1}(s\to t)\) gives

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\Big(E^{-1}(s\to t)x(t)\Big) = E^{-1}(s\to t)\big(\dot x(t)-L(t)x(t)\big). \]

If \(\dot x(t)=L(t)x(t)+r(t)\), then \(\dot x(t)-L(t)x(t)=r(t)\), hence

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\Big(E^{-1}(s\to t)x(t)\Big)=E^{-1}(s\to t)\,r(t). \]

docs.title: A.4 Step 3: integrate from \(s\) to \(t\)
docs.text:
Integrate both sides from \(s\) to \(t\) (use \(\tau\) as the integration variable):

\[ \int_s^t \frac{d}{d\tau}\Big(E^{-1}(s\to \tau)x(\tau)\Big)\,d\tau = \int_s^t E^{-1}(s\to \tau)\,r(\tau)\,d\tau. \]

By the fundamental theorem of calculus, the left-hand side is

\[ E^{-1}(s\to t)x(t)-E^{-1}(s\to s)x(s). \]

Since \(E^{-1}(s\to s)=\exp(0)=1\), we obtain

\[ E^{-1}(s\to t)x(t) = x(s)+\int_s^t E^{-1}(s\to \tau)\,r(\tau)\,d\tau. \]

docs.title: A.5 Step 4: solve for \(x(t)\) (the closed-form formula)
docs.text:
Multiply both sides by \(E(s\to t)\):

\[ x(t)=E(s\to t)x(s)+\int_s^t E(s\to t)\,E^{-1}(s\to \tau)\,r(\tau)\,d\tau. \]

Finally, note that

\[ E(s\to t)\,E^{-1}(s\to \tau) = \exp\!\Big(\int_s^t L(\xi)\,d\xi-\int_s^\tau L(\xi)\,d\xi\Big) = \exp\!\Big(\int_\tau^t L(\xi)\,d\xi\Big) = E(\tau\to t), \]

so the solution can be written as

\[ x(t)=E(s\to t)\,x(s)+\int_s^t E(\tau\to t)\,r(\tau)\,d\tau. \]

docs.title: Appendix B — Derivation of the Fokker–Planck equation (isotropic diffusion)
docs.text:
This appendix derives the Fokker–Planck equation for the diffusion-model-style SDE

\[ dX_t = f(X_t,t)\,dt + g(t)\,dW_t,\qquad X_0\sim p_0, \]

where \(X_t\in\mathbb{R}^D\), \(W_t\) is a standard \(D\)-dimensional Brownian motion, \(f:\mathbb{R}^D\times[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^D\), and \(g:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)\). We assume enough regularity (existence of a smooth density \(p_t\) and sufficient decay at infinity) to justify exchanging derivatives/integrals and integrating by parts.

docs.title: B.0 Notation and assumptions (what we use implicitly)
docs.text:
• Write \(X_t=(X_t^{(1)},\dots,X_t^{(D)})\) and \(W_t=(W_t^{(1)},\dots,W_t^{(D)})\).
  • \(\nabla\varphi=(\partial_{x_1}\varphi,\dots,\partial_{x_D}\varphi)\), \(\Delta\varphi=\sum_{i=1}^D \partial_{x_i x_i}\varphi\), and \(\nabla\!\cdot F=\sum_{i=1}^D \partial_{x_i}F_i\).
  • The quadratic covariation of Brownian motion satisfies
\[ d\langle W^{(i)},W^{(j)}\rangle_t=\delta_{ij}\,dt. \]

Consequently, since \(dX_t^{(i)}=\cdots + g(t)\,dW_t^{(i)}\),

\[ d\langle X^{(i)},X^{(j)}\rangle_t=g(t)^2\,\delta_{ij}\,dt. \]

docs.title: B.1 From Itô’s formula to the generator identity (weak form)
docs.text:
Let \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^D)\) be a smooth test function with compact support. Define the (time-dependent) Itô generator

\[ (\mathcal{L}_t\varphi)(x):= f(x,t)\cdot abla \varphi(x) + rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\,\Delta \varphi(x). \]

Step 1 (Itô’s formula, written component-wise). Since \(X_t\) solves \(dX_t=f(X_t,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t\), Itô’s formula says

\[ d\varphi(X_t) = \sum_{i=1}^D \partial_{x_i}\varphi(X_t)\,dX_t^{(i)} + rac12\sum_{i,j=1}^D \partial_{x_ix_j}\varphi(X_t)\,d\langle X^{(i)},X^{(j)} angle_t. \]

Substitute \(dX_t^{(i)}=f_i(X_t,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t^{(i)}\) and \(d\langle X^{(i)},X^{(j)} angle_t=g(t)^2\delta_{ij}\,dt\):

\[ egin{aligned} d\varphi(X_t) &= \sum_{i=1}^D \partial_{x_i}\varphi(X_t)\, ig(f_i(X_t,t)\,dt+g(t)\,dW_t^{(i)} ig) + rac12\sum_{i,j=1}^D \partial_{x_ix_j}\varphi(X_t)\,g(t)^2\delta_{ij}\,dt \ &= \Big(\sum_{i=1}^D f_i(X_t,t)\,\partial_{x_i}\varphi(X_t)\Big)\,dt + rac12 g(t)^2\Big(\sum_{i=1}^D \partial_{x_ix_i}\varphi(X_t)\Big)\,dt \;+\; g(t)\sum_{i=1}^D \partial_{x_i}\varphi(X_t)\,dW_t^{(i)}. \end{aligned} \]

Recognizing the dot products, this is exactly

\[ d\varphi(X_t) = (\mathcal{L}_t\varphi)(X_t)\,dt + g(t)\, abla\varphi(X_t)\cdot dW_t. \]

Step 2 (integrate and take expectations). Integrate from \(0\) to \(t\):

\[ \varphi(X_t)-\varphi(X_0) = \int_0^t (\mathcal{L}_s\varphi)(X_s)\,ds +\int_0^t g(s)\, abla\varphi(X_s)\cdot dW_s. \]

Taking expectations and using that the Itô stochastic integral is a martingale with zero mean (under standard square-integrability conditions),

\[ rac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] = \mathbb{E} ig[(\mathcal{L}_t\varphi)(X_t) ig]. ag{B.1} \]

This is the weak evolution equation: it characterizes the time derivative of \(\mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)]\) for every test function \(\varphi\).

docs.title: B.2 Convert the generator identity into a PDE for \(p_t\)
docs.text:
If \(X_t\) has density \(p_t\), then

\[ \mathbb{E}[\varphi(X_t)] = \int_{\mathbb{R}^D}\varphi(x)\,p_t(x)\,dx, \qquad \mathbb{E} ig[(\mathcal{L}_t\varphi)(X_t) ig] = \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} (\mathcal{L}_t\varphi)(x)\,p_t(x)\,dx. \]

Plugging into \(( ext{B.1})\) gives

\[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^D}\varphi(x)\,\partial_t p_t(x)\,dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}^D}\Big(f(x,t)\cdot abla\varphi(x) + rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\,\Delta\varphi(x)\Big)p_t(x)\,dx. \]

Step 1 (drift term: one integration by parts). Write the drift term coordinate-wise:

\[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} f\cdot abla\varphi \; p_t\,dx = \sum_{i=1}^D \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} f_i(x,t)\,\partial_{x_i}\varphi(x)\;p_t(x)\,dx. \]

Integrate by parts in \(x_i\) (boundary terms vanish due to compact support/decay):

\[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} f_i\,(\partial_{x_i}\varphi)\,p_t\,dx = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^D} \varphi(x)\,\partial_{x_i} ig(f_i(x,t)\,p_t(x) ig)\,dx. \]

Summing over \(i\) yields

\[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} f\cdot abla\varphi \; p_t\,dx = -\int_{\mathbb{R}^D} \varphi(x)\, abla\!\cdot ig(f(x,t)\,p_t(x) ig)\,dx. \]

Step 2 (diffusion term: two integrations by parts). Since \(g(t)\) does not depend on \(x\), we can factor it out. Using that the Laplacian is formally self-adjoint under these boundary conditions,

\[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} (\Delta\varphi)\;p_t\,dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}^D} \varphi(x)\,\Delta p_t(x)\,dx. \]

One way to see this is coordinate-wise: for each \(i\),

\[ \int (\partial_{x_i x_i}\varphi)\,p_t\,dx = -\int (\partial_{x_i}\varphi)\,(\partial_{x_i}p_t)\,dx = \int \varphi\,(\partial_{x_i x_i}p_t)\,dx, \]

then sum over \(i=1,\dots,D\). Therefore,

\[ \int_{\mathbb{R}^D}\varphi(x)\,\partial_t p_t(x)\,dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}^D}\varphi(x)\Big( - abla\!\cdot(f(x,t)p_t(x)) + rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\,\Delta p_t(x) \Big)\,dx. \]

Since this holds for all \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^D)\), we conclude the Fokker–Planck equation (in the weak sense, and pointwise under additional regularity):

\[ \partial_t p_t(x) = - abla\!\cdot ig(f(x,t)\,p_t(x) ig) + rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\,\Delta p_t(x). ag{FP} \]

docs.title: B.3 Divergence form and the score
docs.text:
The Fokker–Planck equation can be rewritten so that the right-hand side is a single divergence \(- abla\!\cdot( ext{flux})\), making the “mass conservation” structure explicit.

Step 1 (write diffusion as divergence of a flux). Since \(g(t)\) is independent of \(x\),

\[ rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\,\Delta p_t = rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\, abla\!\cdot( abla p_t) = - abla\!\cdot\Big(- rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\, abla p_t\Big) = - abla\!\cdot\Big(- rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\,p_t\, abla\log p_t\Big). \]

In the last equality we used \( abla p_t=p_t abla\log p_t\), valid wherever \(p_t>0\) (and in a weak sense under mild conditions).

Step 2 (combine drift flux and diffusion flux). Substituting into \(( ext{FP})\) yields the pure-divergence form

\[ \partial_t p_t(x) = - abla\!\cdot\Big(f(x,t)\,p_t(x) - rac12 g(t)^2\, abla_x p_t(x)\Big) = - abla\!\cdot\Big(\Big(f(x,t) - rac{1}{2}g(t)^2\, abla_x\log p_t(x)\Big)\,p_t(x)\Big), \]

which matches the common “drift minus diffusion-times-score” decomposition.

Remark (general diffusion matrix). For a general Itô SDE \(dX_t=b\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t\) with \(a=\sigma\sigma^ op\), the diffusion term becomes \( rac12\sum_{ij}\partial_{x_i}\partial_{x_j}(a_{ij}p_t)\). The isotropic case above corresponds to \(a(t,x)=g(t)^2 I\).
